title: Child Health in Primary Care & Home Care
source: Child Health in Primary Care and Home Care_261027_224337.pdf

topics.DEV: Developmental milestones, red flags & MOH screening
topics.ABUSE: Child abuse, SCAN team & sexual abuse

cards.q: When should the full newborn examination be done, and when are the routine postnatal home-visit assessments?
cards.a:
• Complete examination **within 72 hours of birth**
• Home-visit newborn assessments on **day 2, 3, 5, 8-10 and 14-16**
• Explain the aims to parents, share results and record them in the **home-based card** (Buku Pink/Biru)
cards.m: 72 hours = 3 days: examine before the 'day-3 jaundice peak' catches you out.

cards.q: Before examining a newborn at a home visit, what should you review?
cards.a:
• **Parental concerns**
• Family, maternal, antenatal and perinatal history
• Plotted **birth weight and head circumference**
• **Feeding adequacy**
• Passage of **meconium and urine** (and urine stream in a boy)
• **Vitamin K** and immunisation status
• Results of **G6PD** and **cord TSH** screening
cards.m: Feed, Pee, Poo, Vit K, G6PD, TSH: the six boxes to tick before you touch the baby.

cards.q: What are the normal targets for capillary refill and oxygen saturation in a newborn, and the usual heart and respiratory rate ranges?
cards.a:
• Capillary refill time **< 3 seconds**
• SpO2 **> 95% in term** babies; **90-95% in preterm** babies
• Heart rate about **100-160/min**
• Respiratory rate about **40-60/min**; > 60 = tachypnoea
• Temperature **36.5-37.5 °C**
cards.m: Preterm babies are allowed a lower SpO2 target (90-95%) because hyperoxia damages the retina (ROP).

cards.q: What three questions should you ask the mother early in the newborn check, and why does the stool question matter?
cards.a:
• Has the baby **passed stool** in the first 24 h?
• Has the baby **passed urine** in the first 24 h?
• Has **breastfeeding started**?
• Failure to pass **meconium by 24-48 h** suggests **Hirschsprung disease**, meconium ileus or anorectal malformation
• No urine by 24 h: think **posterior urethral valves** (boys) or renal anomaly
cards.m: No poo by 48 h = think Hirschsprung (and later, think Down syndrome association).

cards.q: Caput succedaneum vs cephalohaematoma vs subaponeurotic (subgaleal) haemorrhage: how do you tell them apart?
cards.a:
• **Caput**: soft scalp oedema present at birth, **crosses suture lines**, resolves in days
• **Cephalohaematoma**: subperiosteal bleed, **does not cross sutures**, appears after hours, may take weeks; adds to **jaundice**
• **Subaponeurotic haemorrhage**: fluctuant boggy swelling that **crosses sutures** and spreads to the neck/ears; can cause **hypovolaemic shock**
cards.m: Cephalohaematoma is Confined by sutures; Caput and subgaleal Cross them, but only subgaleal kills.

cards.q: Why is a subaponeurotic haemorrhage an emergency, and what should a KK doctor do on finding one?
cards.a:
• The subaponeurotic space is large and unconfined, so a baby can lose a **large share of its blood volume** into it
• Signs: enlarging boggy scalp, pallor, tachycardia, poor perfusion, later jaundice
• Often follows **vacuum (ventouse) delivery**
• Action: **urgent hospital referral** for monitoring of head circumference, Hb, coagulation and fluid/blood resuscitation
cards.m: Ventouse + boggy scalp + pale baby = bleed into the scalp: send now.

cards.q: A newborn has a firm, non-tender lump in one sternomastoid muscle with the head tilted. What is it and how is it managed?
cards.a:
• **Sternomastoid tumour** (fibrosis of the muscle, often after a difficult delivery)
• Causes **congenital muscular torticollis**: head tilts towards and chin turns away from the lesion
• Management: parent-taught **passive stretching / physiotherapy**; most resolve in months
• Refer if not improving, to prevent **plagiocephaly** and facial asymmetry
cards.m: Tumour that is not a tumour: stretch, do not cut.

cards.q: An absent or white red reflex is found during a newborn examination. What are the key causes and the next step?
cards.a:
• **Congenital cataract** (think congenital rubella, galactosaemia, Down syndrome)
• **Retinoblastoma** (leukocoria)
• Congenital glaucoma, retinal detachment, vitreous haemorrhage
• Next step: **urgent ophthalmology referral**; early surgery prevents **amblyopia** in cataract
cards.m: White pupil = 'white reflex is a red flag'.

cards.q: What is the significance of pre-auricular pits, skin tags or low-set ears on the newborn check?
cards.a:
• Linked with **hearing loss**: make sure the **UNHS** (AABR/OAE) is done
• May accompany **renal anomalies** and branchial arch syndromes
• Low-set ears with other dysmorphism suggest a **chromosomal syndrome** (e.g., trisomies)
• Isolated pits may later form a **pre-auricular sinus** that gets infected
cards.m: Ears and kidneys form at the same time: odd ears, check hearing (and think kidneys).

cards.q: Which newborn oral findings are benign, and which need action?
cards.a:
• **Epstein pearls**: white keratin cysts on the palate, benign, resolve
• **Oral thrush**: white plaques that do not wipe off easily, treat with **nystatin** drops
• **Natal teeth**: remove if loose (**aspiration risk**) or causing feeding problems
• **Tongue tie**: frenotomy only if it impairs **breastfeeding**
• **Cleft lip/palate**: feeding support and refer to cleft team
• **Macroglossia**: think hypothyroidism, Beckwith-Wiedemann, Down syndrome
cards.m: Pearls are pretty and pass; plaques need nystatin.

cards.q: What are the signs of respiratory distress in a newborn?
cards.a:
• **Tachypnoea** (RR > 60/min)
• **Grunting** (expiration against a partly closed glottis to keep alveoli open)
• **Nasal flaring**
• **Retractions** (subcostal, intercostal, sternal recession)
• Cyanosis; **stridor** suggests upper airway obstruction
• Any of these in a home visit = **refer**
cards.m: Grunt, Flare, Retract, Fast: GFRF.

cards.q: How do you distinguish umbilical granuloma, patent urachus and omphalitis?
cards.a:
• **Umbilical granuloma**: moist pink fleshy nodule after cord separation; treat with **silver nitrate** or salt, good cord hygiene
• **Patent urachus**: clear fluid (**urine**) leaking from the umbilicus, worse on crying; refer to surgeons
• **Omphalitis**: **redness spreading** around the umbilicus, discharge, smell, fever; risk of sepsis, needs **IV antibiotics**
• **Umbilical hernia**: reducible bulge, most close spontaneously
cards.m: Granuloma = pink and wet; urachus = wee from the belly button; omphalitis = red and spreading.

cards.q: What does a tuft of hair, lipoma, haemangioma or deep dimple over the lower spine suggest, and what do you do?
cards.a:
• Markers of **occult spinal dysraphism** (spina bifida occulta, tethered cord)
• Examine the legs, anal tone and bladder function
• Arrange **spinal ultrasound** (best in the first months) and refer to paediatrics/neurosurgery
• A simple shallow dimple within the natal cleft is usually benign
cards.m: Skin on the back tells tales about the cord beneath.

cards.q: Why must femoral pulses be palpated at the newborn check?
cards.a:
• Weak, delayed or absent femoral pulses suggest **coarctation of the aorta**
• Coarctation may present when the **ductus arteriosus closes** (days 2-7) with shock or heart failure
• Compare with the right brachial pulse; check pre- and post-ductal SpO2
• Action: **urgent paediatric referral** and echocardiography
cards.m: No femorals = think 'Coarct', especially in a girl with Turner features.

cards.q: A baby boy has hypospadias. What important advice do you give the parents?
cards.a:
• **Do not circumcise**: the foreskin is used in surgical repair
• Check for **chordee** and both testes; hypospadias with **impalpable testes** needs urgent assessment for a **disorder of sex development** (e.g., CAH)
• Refer to paediatric surgery/urology; repair usually in infancy (around 6-18 months)
cards.m: Hypospadias: the foreskin is spare parts, keep it.

cards.q: An undescended testis is found on the newborn exam. What is the plan?
cards.a:
• Many descend spontaneously in the **first 3-6 months**
• Review; if still undescended by about **6 months**, refer to paediatric surgery
• **Orchidopexy** ideally by **12-18 months** to protect fertility and allow cancer surveillance
• **Bilateral impalpable testes** in a newborn: urgent referral (exclude DSD/CAH)
cards.m: Down by 6 months, or the surgeon by 1 year.

cards.q: A mother is worried about whitish vaginal discharge or slight vaginal bleeding in her 5-day-old daughter. What is it?
cards.a:
• Usually physiological, caused by **withdrawal of maternal oestrogen** after birth
• White mucoid discharge and small **pseudomenses** are common in the first 1-2 weeks
• Also explains **breast swelling** in newborns of both sexes
• Reassure; review if heavy bleeding, persistent beyond a few weeks or other bleeding signs (check vitamin K)
cards.m: Mum's hormones leave, baby has a mini-period.

cards.q: Barlow vs Ortolani manoeuvre: what does each test?
cards.a:
• **Barlow**: hip adducted, gentle **posterior pressure** tries to **dislocate** a located but unstable hip; clunk = dislocatable
• **Ortolani**: hip **abducted** with pressure from behind on the proximal thigh to **relocate** an already dislocated head; clunk = reduction
• Both screen for **developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH)**; also look for **asymmetrical skin folds** and limb length
cards.m: Barlow = Back and out (dislocates); Ortolani = Out to in (relocates).

cards.q: What are the risk factors for developmental dysplasia of the hip, and what follow-up is needed if a hip is unstable?
cards.a:
• Risk factors: **breech presentation**, **female**, **family history**, first-born, oligohydramnios, other packaging deformities (e.g., talipes, torticollis)
• Unstable or clicking hip on exam: refer for **hip ultrasound** (around 4-6 weeks) and orthopaedics
• Treatment if confirmed: **Pavlik harness**
• Late signs: limited abduction, leg-length discrepancy, limp
cards.m: The 4 Fs: Female, First-born, Family history, Feet first (breech).

cards.q: How do you tell congenital talipes equinovarus (CTEV) from positional talipes?
cards.a:
• **Positional talipes**: foot can be **passively corrected** to neutral; from intrauterine posture; resolves with stretching
• **CTEV** (club foot): **rigid** equinus, varus and adduction that **cannot be corrected**; skin creases, small calf
• CTEV: early orthopaedic referral for **Ponseti serial casting**
• Examine hips (DDH association) and spine
cards.m: If you can push it straight, it is posture; if not, it is Ponseti.

cards.q: Describe the Moro reflex, when it disappears, and the meaning of an asymmetric response.
cards.a:
• Startle response: head extends, **arms and legs extend and abduct**, baby cries, then **arms adduct** back
• Normally disappears by about **4-6 months**. Note: slide says 'about 2 months'; most references put it at 3-6 months
• **Asymmetric**: **Erb palsy** (brachial plexus injury) or **fractured clavicle/humerus**
• **Absent** in a newborn: CNS depression; **persistent** beyond 6 months: possible cerebral palsy
cards.m: Moro: 'open up, then hug'. One arm will not open = check the clavicle and the brachial plexus.

cards.q: Palmar vs plantar grasp reflex: what is the normal timing and what does persistence suggest?
cards.a:
• Stroking the palm makes the fingers close in a grasp
• **Palmar grasp** lasts until about **5-6 months** (many texts say 3-4 months)
• **Plantar (toe) grasp** lasts until **9-12 months**, until the child walks
• **Persistence** beyond these ages or asymmetry suggests an **upper motor neurone problem** such as cerebral palsy
• Hand grasp must fade before **voluntary reaching and grasping**
cards.m: Hands let go before feet: palm by about 6 months, toes by about 12.

cards.q: What are the normal birth anthropometric values for a term baby, and why are they plotted?
cards.a:
• Weight about **2.5-4.0 kg** (low birth weight **< 2500 g**)
• Length about **50 cm**
• Head circumference about **33-35 cm**
• Plot on the **WHO growth chart** in the Child Health Record Book
• Baseline to detect **microcephaly/macrocephaly**, SGA/LGA and later growth faltering
cards.m: Term baby rule of thumb: 3 kg, 50 cm, 35 cm head.

cards.q: What is the Ballard score and what does it assess?
cards.a:
• Clinical estimate of **gestational age** (about 20-44 weeks with the New Ballard)
• **Neuromuscular maturity** (6): posture, square window, arm recoil, popliteal angle, scarf sign, heel-to-ear
• **Physical maturity** (6): skin, lanugo, plantar creases, breast, eye/ear, genitalia
• Total score converts to weeks; most accurate in the **first 12-24 hours** (or up to 96 h)
• Term = **37 to < 42 weeks**; preterm < 37 weeks
cards.m: Ballard = 6 + 6: six for Muscles, six for Maturity of the skin and body.

cards.q: How common is neonatal jaundice, and at what bilirubin level does it become clinically visible?
cards.a:
• **Most common** newborn condition
• Occurs in **50-75% of term** and **> 80% of preterm** babies
• Clinically visible when serum bilirubin **> 85 µmol/L (5 mg/dL)**
• More common in **Asian** babies; varies with race
cards.m: 85 µmol/L = 5 mg/dL: the 'visible line'.

cards.q: Why is jaundice appearing within 24 hours of life always pathological, and what are the likely causes?
cards.a:
• Physiological jaundice never appears before 24 h, so early jaundice means **excess production** or disease
• Likely causes: **haemolysis** from **ABO incompatibility**, **Rh isoimmunisation**, **G6PD deficiency**, spherocytosis
• Also **sepsis** and congenital infection (TORCH)
• Needs **urgent** TSB measurement and hospital referral
cards.m: Day 1 yellow = danger fellow.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of physiological jaundice?
cards.a:
• **Increased bilirubin production**: higher haemoglobin and **shorter red cell life span** (about 70-90 days vs 120)
• **Liver immaturity**: low UDP-glucuronyl transferase activity, so poor conjugation and clearance
• Increased **enterohepatic circulation** (gut beta-glucuronidase, sterile gut)
• Result: unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
cards.m: More made, less cleared, more recycled.

cards.q: What is the typical time course of physiological neonatal jaundice?
cards.a:
• Appears **2-4 days** after birth
• Resolves within **1-2 weeks** in term babies
• Up to **3 weeks** in preterm babies
• Baby otherwise **well**, feeding well, normal stools and urine
cards.m: Starts after day 1, gone by week 2 (term) or week 3 (preterm).

cards.q: List the features that make neonatal jaundice pathological.
cards.a:
• Onset **< 24 hours** of life
• **Rapid rise**: > **103 µmol/L per 24 h** (6 mg/dL/day) or > **8.5 µmol/L per hour** (0.5 mg/dL/h)
• **Conjugated bilirubin > 34 µmol/L** (2 mg/dL)
• **Prolonged**: > 14 days in term, > 21 days in preterm
• Plus: unwell baby, pale stools/dark urine, high bilirubin for age
cards.m: EARLY, FAST, DIRECT, LONG: any one makes it pathological.

cards.q: What are the causes of pathological unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia?
cards.a:
• **Haemolysis/increased production**: ABO incompatibility, Rh isoimmunisation, **G6PD deficiency**, hereditary spherocytosis, **cephalohaematoma**, severe bruising, **polycythaemia**
• **Decreased clearance**: **hypothyroidism**
• **Increased enterohepatic circulation**: **breast milk jaundice**, GI obstruction
cards.m: Made too much (haemolysis, bruises, polycythaemia), cleared too slowly (thyroid), recycled (breast milk, obstruction).

cards.q: ABO incompatibility vs Rh isoimmunisation: what are the key differences?
cards.a:
• **ABO**: mother **group O**, baby A or B; maternal anti-A/anti-B IgG; **can occur in the first pregnancy** (common in primigravida); usually milder
• **Rh**: mother **Rh-negative**, baby Rh-positive; needs **prior sensitisation**, so usually affects **later** pregnancies; can be severe (hydrops)
• Both: **direct Coombs test positive**, early jaundice
• Rh disease is prevented by **anti-D** for Rh-negative mothers
cards.m: ABO: first baby can be hit. Rh: the second baby pays for the first.

cards.q: Why does G6PD deficiency matter so much in Malaysian neonates, and what advice do parents need?
cards.a:
• **X-linked**, so mostly **boys**; common in Malaysia; detected by **cord blood screening**
• Causes **sudden, severe haemolytic NNJ** and kernicterus risk
• Avoid triggers: **naphthalene (mothballs)**, some **herbal remedies** (e.g., certain Chinese herbs), oxidant drugs such as **sulphonamides**, primaquine, nitrofurantoin; **fava beans**
• Give a G6PD alert card; early review if jaundice appears
cards.m: G6PD: 'Mothballs, herbs and beans make the red cells burst'.

cards.q: Breastfeeding (suboptimal intake) jaundice vs breast milk jaundice: how do they differ?
cards.a:
• **Suboptimal intake jaundice**: first week, poor feeding, **weight loss**, dehydration; fix by **more frequent effective breastfeeds** (8-12/day)
• **Breast milk jaundice**: thriving baby, **starts late in week 1, peaks at 2-3 weeks**, can last weeks; increased enterohepatic circulation
• Bilirubin falls if breastfeeding is suspended for 24-48 h, but this is **not recommended routinely**: continue breastfeeding after excluding other causes
• Note: slide says it is 'suspected when suspending breastfeeding'; correct is that it is **suggested by a fall in bilirubin** when feeds are paused, and is a **diagnosis of exclusion**
cards.m: Too little milk early = feeding problem; the milk itself late = breast milk jaundice.

cards.q: What are the causes of conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in a neonate?
cards.a:
• **Biliary obstruction**: **biliary atresia**, choledochal cyst
• **Infection**: sepsis, **UTI**, meningitis, **TORCH**
• **Neonatal hepatitis**
• (Also metabolic causes, e.g., galactosaemia)
• Defined as conjugated bilirubin **> 34 µmol/L (2 mg/dL)**
cards.m: Conjugated = the liver did its job but bile cannot get out: block, bug or hepatitis.

cards.q: What features suggest biliary atresia and why is the timing of referral critical?
cards.a:
• **Prolonged jaundice** with **pale (acholic) stools**, **dark urine** that stains the nappy, hepatomegaly; baby may look well
• **Conjugated** hyperbilirubinaemia
• **Kasai portoenterostomy** works best **before 60 days** of age; late surgery leads to cirrhosis and transplant
• Use the **stool colour card** in the Child Health Record Book
• Action: **urgent** paediatric/surgical referral
cards.m: Pale poo + dark wee + yellow after 2 weeks = biliary atresia until proven otherwise; Kasai before 60 days.

cards.q: Define prolonged neonatal jaundice.
cards.a:
• **Visible jaundice** (SB > 85 µmol/L or 5 mg/dL)
• Persisting beyond **14 days** of life in a **term** baby
• Or beyond **21 days** in a **preterm** baby
cards.m: Term 2 weeks, preterm 3 weeks.

cards.q: A 3-week-old term baby is still jaundiced. What should be done at the Klinik Kesihatan?
cards.a:
• Ask about **stool and urine colour** (compare stool card), feeding, weight gain
• Measure **total and conjugated (direct) bilirubin**
• Check **G6PD** and **cord TSH** results (or do TFT)
• **Urine** dipstick/culture for UTI; FBC if pale
• Conjugated > 34 µmol/L or pale stools: **urgent referral**
• Unconjugated, well, thriving, breastfed: likely breast milk jaundice; continue breastfeeding and review
cards.m: Prolonged jaundice: Split it (conjugated or not), Stools, Screens (G6PD, TSH), Sepsis (urine).

cards.q: How does severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia damage the brain?
cards.a:
• **Unconjugated bilirubin** is **lipid-soluble**; free (unbound) bilirubin **crosses the blood-brain barrier**
• Deposits in the **basal ganglia** (globus pallidus), hippocampus, brainstem auditory and oculomotor nuclei
• Acute stage: **acute bilirubin encephalopathy (ABE)**
• Permanent stage: **chronic bilirubin encephalopathy / kernicterus**
• Risk higher with prematurity, acidosis, sepsis, hypoalbuminaemia
cards.m: Unconjugated = fat-loving, so it slips into the fatty brain.

cards.q: What are the classic features of chronic bilirubin encephalopathy (kernicterus)?
cards.a:
• **Choreoathetoid (dyskinetic) cerebral palsy**
• **Sensorineural hearing loss** / auditory neuropathy
• **Upward gaze palsy**
• **Dental enamel dysplasia**
• Variable intellectual impairment
cards.m: Kernicterus tetrad: Moves (athetosis), Ears (deaf), Eyes (gaze up), Teeth (enamel).

cards.q: What are the signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy by phase?
cards.a:
• **Early**: lethargy, **hypotonia**, poor suck
• **Intermediate**: irritability, **hypertonia** (retrocollis, **opisthotonus**), **high-pitched cry**, fever
• **Advanced**: apnoea, **seizures**, coma, deep stupor
• Any sign = **emergency**: intensive phototherapy and prepare for **exchange transfusion**
cards.m: Floppy, then stiff and shrill, then fitting.

cards.q: What is the BIND score and how is it interpreted?
cards.a:
• **Bilirubin-Induced Neurologic Dysfunction** score: grades **acute bilirubin encephalopathy**
• Three items, each scored 0-3: **mental status**, **muscle tone**, **cry pattern**
• Total **1-3 = mild**, **4-6 = moderate**, **7-9 = severe** ABE
• Moderate ABE is often reversible with urgent **exchange transfusion**; severe ABE usually leaves kernicterus
cards.m: BIND looks at the baby's 'Brain, Body, Bawl': alertness, tone, cry.

cards.q: What are the risk factors for severe neonatal jaundice?
cards.a:
• **Prematurity**, low birth weight
• Jaundice in the **first 24 h**; **rapid rise** of TSB; **high pre-discharge** bilirubin
• Mother **group O** or **Rh-negative**; **G6PD deficiency**
• **Sepsis**; **cephalohaematoma** or bruises
• **Excessive weight loss**, **lactation failure** in exclusive breastfeeding
• **Infant of diabetic mother**; **sibling** with severe NNJ
cards.m: 'Small, early, fast, O-negative, G6PD, bruised, septic, starving, sugar-baby, sibling'.

cards.q: What should you look for when examining a jaundiced newborn?
cards.a:
• General condition, gestation, weight, **signs of sepsis**, **hydration**
• Signs of **acute bilirubin encephalopathy** (BIND score)
• **Pallor** (haemolysis), **plethora** (polycythaemia), **cephalohaematoma**, subaponeurotic haemorrhage
• Signs of **intrauterine infection**: petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly
• **Cephalocaudal extent** of jaundice (Kramer)
cards.m: Sick? Dry? Brain? Blood (pale/plethoric/bruised)? Bugs (TORCH)? How far down?

cards.q: How is Kramer's visual assessment of jaundice performed?
cards.a:
• In good (preferably **natural**) light, **blanch the skin** with gentle finger pressure and note the underlying yellow colour
• Jaundice usually visible at about **86-120 µmol/L (5-7 mg/dL)**
• Spreads **cephalocaudally** (head to toe) as bilirubin rises
• Kramer's rule links the **extent** of skin staining to the approximate serum level
cards.m: Jaundice is like water filling a bottle upside down: it starts at the head and pours to the toes.

cards.q: What are the five Kramer zones and their approximate serum bilirubin levels?
cards.a:
• Zone 1 **head and neck**: about **100 µmol/L**
• Zone 2 **upper trunk** (to umbilicus): about **150 µmol/L**
• Zone 3 **lower trunk and thighs** (to knees): about **200 µmol/L**
• Zone 4 **arms and lower legs**: about **250 µmol/L**
• Zone 5 **palms and soles**: **> 250 µmol/L**
• Visual estimates are unreliable (especially in darker skin), so confirm with **TcB/TSB**
cards.m: Add 50 for each zone down: 100, 150, 200, 250, then palms and soles above 250.

cards.q: When should transcutaneous bilirubin (TcB) and total serum bilirubin (TSB) be used?
cards.a:
• Use **TcB** whenever jaundice is detected
• If **TcB > 200 µmol/L (12 mg/dL)**, measure **TSB**
• If TcB is **not available**, measure **TSB** in every jaundiced baby
• Plot TSB on the **hour-specific treatment chart** for gestation and risk factors
cards.m: TcB is the screening torch; above 200, call in the blood test.

cards.q: Why should TcB not be used to monitor babies on phototherapy?
cards.a:
• Phototherapy **bleaches bilirubin in the skin** first
• TcB then **underestimates** the serum level, giving false reassurance
• Monitor with **TSB** during and soon after phototherapy
cards.m: The light cleans the skin before it cleans the blood.

cards.q: Which tests are needed for early-onset (< 24 h), rapidly rising (> 8.5 µmol/L/h) or severe jaundice?
cards.a:
• **G6PD** (if not already screened)
• **Mother's and baby's blood groups**
• **Direct Coombs test**
• **FBC ± peripheral blood film**
• **Reticulocyte count**
• **Septic workup** if infection suspected
cards.m: Groups, Coombs, Count, Retics, G6PD, Germs.

cards.q: How does phototherapy work and what are its side effects?
cards.a:
• Blue-green light (about 460-490 nm) converts unconjugated bilirubin into **water-soluble isomers (e.g., lumirubin)** that are excreted in **bile and urine without conjugation**
• Side effects: **insensible water loss**/dehydration, loose stools, rash, temperature instability, separation from mother
• **Bronze baby** syndrome if conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
• Cover the **eyes**, maximise skin exposure, keep breastfeeding
cards.m: Light turns the 'fat-soluble' pigment into a 'water-soluble' one that can be washed out.

cards.q: What treatments exist beyond phototherapy for severe neonatal jaundice?
cards.a:
• **Exchange transfusion** (usually **double-volume**, about 160-180 mL/kg): for TSB above the ET line, signs of ABE, or rise despite intensive phototherapy (slide: > **8.5 µmol/L/h**)
• **IV immunoglobulin**: isoimmune haemolysis (Rh/ABO, Coombs positive) to reduce need for ET
• **Human albumin**: binds free bilirubin
• **Clofibrate**: enzyme inducer (limited use)
• Note: the slide lists rate of rise as the stand-alone indication; in practice thresholds come from TSB-for-age charts
cards.m: ET swaps the baby's yellow blood; IVIG stops the antibodies chewing the cells.

cards.q: What home-care advice should be given to parents of a mildly jaundiced breastfed baby?
cards.a:
• **Breastfeed frequently** (8-12 times/day); do not give plain water or glucose water
• Do **not** rely on **sunlight** exposure to treat jaundice
• Avoid **G6PD triggers** (mothballs, herbal remedies) if deficient
• Return urgently if: jaundice spreads **below the umbilicus**/to palms and soles, baby is **lethargic or feeding poorly**, **pale stools or dark urine**, jaundice beyond **2 weeks**
• Attend scheduled home visits/KK reviews
cards.m: Feed more, no sunbathing, watch the poo, come back if yellow spreads.

cards.q: What are the four functional developmental domains?
cards.a:
• **Gross motor**: head control, rolling, sitting, crawling, walking, running, stairs
• **Fine motor and vision**: tracking, palmar then pincer grasp, cube stacking, scribbling
• **Speech and hearing**: sound localisation, babbling, words, sentences
• **Social and self-help**: smiling, games, pretend play, cup drinking, feeding, dressing
cards.m: 'Go, Fiddle, Talk, Play'.

cards.q: What milestones are expected at 6 weeks?
cards.a:
• **Gross motor**: lifts head briefly when prone
• **Vision**: fixes on and follows a face/object
• **Social**: **responsive (social) smile** by about 6 weeks
• Note: slide says 'follows object across midline'; at 6 weeks babies typically follow to the midline (about 90°), and **follow through 180°** by about **3 months**
cards.m: Six weeks = Smile.

cards.q: What milestones are expected between 3 and 6 months?
cards.a:
• **Good head control** (no head lag by about 4 months)
• **Rolls** front to back (about 4-5 months)
• **Transfers objects** hand to hand (about 6 months), reaches and grasps with palm
• **Tuneful babbling**, laughs, squeals
cards.m: By 6 months the baby Rolls, Reaches, Transfers and Babbles.

cards.q: What milestones are expected at 9 months?
cards.a:
• **Sits without support** (steady)
• **Inferior pincer grasp**
• **Responds to name**; babbles mama/dada non-specifically
• **Plays peek-a-boo**; stranger anxiety
• Crawling, pulls to stand
cards.m: Nine months: Sits, Pinches (inferior), Peeks-a-boo, knows its Name.

cards.q: What milestones are expected at 12 months?
cards.a:
• **Cruises** along furniture or **stands alone**; may take first steps
• **Neat pincer grasp**
• Speaks **1-3 words** with meaning
• **Drinks from a cup**; waves bye-bye, points
cards.m: First birthday: First words, First steps, Fine pincer.

cards.q: What milestones are expected at 18 months?
cards.a:
• **Walks unassisted**
• Builds a **tower of 2-3 cubes** (many texts say 3-4)
• Has about **10-20 words**
• **Feeds self with a spoon**
• **Simple pretend play**; points to show interest
cards.m: 18 months: walks, spoons, and has more words than its age in months would suggest.

cards.q: What milestones are expected at 2 years?
cards.a:
• **Runs** steadily; climbs stairs **2 feet per step**
• **Tower of 6 cubes**
• **Joins 2 words** (e.g., 'Nak susu')
• **Indicates toilet needs**
cards.m: Two years: 2-word phrases, 2 feet per step, 6 cubes (3 x 2).

cards.q: What milestones are expected at 3 years?
cards.a:
• **Stands on one foot** briefly; **rides a tricycle**
• **Copies a circle**
• Speaks in **3-4 word sentences**; asks 'Why?'
• **Dresses with minimal help**; interactive play
cards.m: Three years: 3 wheels, 3-word sentences, a round 'O' (circle).

cards.q: What is the normal age range for independent sitting and walking, and when does each become a red flag?
cards.a:
• **Sitting** without support: usually **6-8 months**, steady by 9 months; red flag: **not sitting by 9-12 months**
• **Walking** alone: usually **12-15 months** (range about 9-18); red flag: **not walking by 18 months**
• Late walker (especially a boy): check **CK** for Duchenne muscular dystrophy, hips (DDH) and tone (cerebral palsy)
cards.m: Sit by 9, walk by 18: double it to remember.

cards.q: How does grasp and fine motor skill progress over the first 3 years?
cards.a:
• Palmar grasp and reaching: **4-6 months**
• **Transfers** hand to hand: about **6 months**
• **Inferior pincer**: **9 months**; **neat pincer**: **12 months**
• Tower of **2-3 cubes** at 18 months, **6 cubes** at 2 years, about **9 cubes** at 3 years
• Drawing: copies **circle 3 y**, **cross 4 y**, **square 4.5 y**, **triangle 5 y**
cards.m: Shapes by age: Circle 3, Cross 4, Square 4.5, Triangle 5.

cards.q: How does expressive language develop from 6 months to 3 years?
cards.a:
• **6 months**: tuneful babbling
• **9 months**: mama/dada non-specific, responds to name
• **12 months**: **1-3 words** with meaning
• **18 months**: **10-20 words**
• **2 years**: **2-word phrases**
• **3 years**: **3-4 word sentences**, asks 'why'
cards.m: From 1 year: 1 word, 2 years: 2 words together, 3 years: 3-4 word sentences.

cards.q: What are the developmental red flags from 6 weeks to 6 months?
cards.a:
• **No eye contact**: fails to fix on or track faces
• **Persistent fisting**: hands tightly clenched (thumb in palm) beyond about 3 months
• **Poor head control**: floppy neck by 6 months
• **No vocalisation**: absent smiles or cooing
cards.m: Early red flags: no Look, no Smile, Fist closed, Floppy head.

cards.q: What are the developmental red flags from 9 to 18 months?
cards.a:
• **Unable to sit** without support by 9-12 months
• **Not walking** alone by 18 months
• **No meaningful words** by 18 months
• **No pointing** or sharing of interest (think ASD)
• (Also: no babbling by 12 months)
cards.m: 18 months: no Walk, no Words, no Pointing = refer.

cards.q: What are the developmental red flags at 2 years and at any age?
cards.a:
• **No spontaneous 2-word phrases** by 2 years
• **Does not follow simple commands**
• **Regression**: loss of previously acquired speech, social or motor skills at **any age**
• Regression always needs **urgent** specialist referral (e.g., ASD, Rett syndrome, neurodegenerative or metabolic disease, epilepsy)
cards.m: Losing a skill is worse than being late for one.

cards.q: Why is a clear hand preference before 12-18 months a red flag?
cards.a:
• Children normally use **both hands** until about 18 months; handedness emerges later (around 2-3 years)
• Early preference usually means the **other hand is weak**
• Suggests **hemiplegic cerebral palsy** or brachial plexus injury
• Examine tone, power and reflexes of the neglected side; refer
cards.m: An early 'right-hander' may really be a weak 'left-hander'.

cards.q: A 2-year-old has delayed speech but normal motor milestones. What is the first investigation?
cards.a:
• **Formal hearing assessment** (audiology), even if newborn hearing screening was passed
• Hearing loss is a common, treatable cause of speech delay
• Then assess **social communication** (ASD screen, e.g., M-CHAT), oromotor function, environment and global development
• Refer to **speech and language therapy** early
cards.m: Speech late? Test the ears first.

cards.q: Define global developmental delay.
cards.a:
• Significant delay in **two or more developmental domains** (gross/fine motor, speech/language, cognition, social/personal, activities of daily living)
• Used for children **under 5 years**
• Older children who are formally tested are labelled **intellectual disability** instead
• Needs paediatric referral, hearing/vision check and aetiological workup (e.g., TFT, chromosomes)
cards.m: Global = two or more domains, under five.

cards.q: How do you assess the development of a child who was born preterm?
cards.a:
• Use **corrected age** = chronological age minus weeks born early
• Correct until about **2 years** of age
• Example: a baby born at 32 weeks is 8 weeks premature, so at 6 months old is judged against 4-month milestones
• Note: **immunisations** follow **chronological** age, not corrected age
cards.m: Milestones: correct the age. Vaccines: do not.

cards.q: What is the Universal Newborn Hearing Screening (UNHS) programme?
cards.a:
• Mandatory MOH screening for **congenital hearing loss**
• Tests: **AABR** (automated auditory brainstem response) or **OAE** (otoacoustic emissions)
• Done **before hospital discharge** or within the **first month** of life
• Aim (1-3-6): screen by 1 month, diagnose by 3 months, intervene by 6 months
cards.m: 1-3-6: screen by 1, diagnose by 3, fit aids by 6 months.

cards.q: At which ages is the M-CHAT autism screen done in primary care?
cards.a:
• MOH ASD CPG: **18 months** (early identification) and **24 months** (to pick up children who regress)
• M-CHAT is validated for about **16-30 months**
• Note: slide p36 says 18 and 36 months; correct is **18 and 24 months** (as on slide p64), since 36 months is outside the M-CHAT age range
cards.m: M-CHAT is a toddler tool: 18 and 24 months.

cards.q: What is the role of the Child Health Record Book (Buku Pink / Buku Biru)?
cards.a:
• **Home-based record** kept by parents (pink for girls, blue for boys)
• Covers **routine scheduled visits from 0-6 years** (slide: 15 visits)
• Used for **growth charting**, **immunisations** and **milestone** checks
• Also holds screening results (G6PD, TSH, hearing) and the **stool colour card**
cards.m: The baby's passport: bring it to every visit.

cards.q: How do social and self-help skills progress from 6 weeks to 3 years?
cards.a:
• **6 weeks**: responsive smile
• **9 months**: peek-a-boo, stranger awareness
• **12 months**: drinks from a cup, waves bye-bye
• **18 months**: feeds self with a spoon, simple pretend play
• **2 years**: indicates toilet needs
• **3 years**: dresses with minimal help, interactive play
cards.m: Smile, Peek, Cup, Spoon, Toilet, Dress: one step every few months.

cards.q: A developmental red flag is detected at a KKIA check. What is the next step?
cards.a:
• Do **not 'wait and see'**
• Check **hearing and vision**, growth and **head circumference**, dysmorphism, neurological exam (tone, reflexes), and look for regression
• Refer to a **paediatrician / Child Development Centre** for full assessment
• Start **early intervention** in parallel (therapy, PDK) rather than waiting for a label
• Counsel parents and arrange follow-up
cards.m: Red flag = Refer + Rehab now, Reassure never.

cards.q: What is the absolute contraindication to any vaccine?
cards.a:
• **Severe anaphylactic reaction** to a **previous dose** of the same vaccine
• Or anaphylaxis to a **component** of the vaccine (e.g., neomycin, gelatin)
• Applies to both live and killed vaccines
• Everything else is a precaution or a false contraindication
cards.m: Only anaphylaxis says a permanent 'never' to a vaccine.

cards.q: In which children are live vaccines (e.g., BCG, MMR) contraindicated?
cards.a:
• **Immunosuppressed** children: **malignancy**, **leukaemia**, **lymphoma**, **irradiation**, chemotherapy
• **Post-transplant**
• **Primary immunodeficiency** syndromes
• High-dose systemic steroids (see separate card)
• Killed/inactivated vaccines remain **safe** (may give a weaker response)
cards.m: Live vaccine in a weak host can become a real infection.

cards.q: Why are live vaccines avoided in pregnancy, and when is the rule broken?
cards.a:
• **Theoretical risk to the fetus** from the live organism
• Exception: **significant exposure** to serious disease such as **polio** or **yellow fever**, when the benefit outweighs the risk
• A **child's mother being pregnant** is NOT a reason to withhold a child's vaccines
cards.m: Pregnant woman: avoid live. Pregnant mum of the baby: vaccinate the baby.

cards.q: Acute febrile illness vs mild illness without fever: which delays immunisation?
cards.a:
• **Acute febrile (moderate to severe) illness**: **postpone** until recovered, so a fever is not blamed on the vaccine and vice versa
• **Mild illness without fever** (mild diarrhoea, cough, runny nose): **vaccinate as scheduled**
• Missing a dose for a cold is a common missed opportunity
cards.m: Snotty but not hot = vaccinate.

cards.q: What is the rule on timing between the Mantoux (tuberculin skin) test and MMR?
cards.a:
• If a Mantoux is planned, give it **before or on the same day** as MMR
• After a Mantoux, **delay MMR until the test has been read** (48-72 h)
• After MMR, wait **at least 4 weeks** before a Mantoux
• Reason: measles vaccine **suppresses cell-mediated immunity**, causing a **false-negative** Mantoux
cards.m: MMR muffles the Mantoux for a month.

cards.q: When is a further dose of a killed (inactivated) vaccine contraindicated?
cards.a:
• Generally **safe**
• Contraindicated after a **severe local reaction** in a previous dose: induration involving **more than 2/3 of the limb**
• Or a **severe generalised reaction** to a previous dose
• Minor redness and soreness are not contraindications
cards.m: Killed vaccines: stop only if the last dose swelled two-thirds of the limb or floored the child.

cards.q: Which common skin, respiratory and drug situations are NOT contraindications to vaccination?
cards.a:
• **Mild illness without fever**: mild diarrhoea, cough, runny nose
• **Asthma, eczema, hay fever, impetigo, heat rash** (just avoid injecting into affected skin)
• Treatment with **antibiotics**, **topical** or **inhaled steroids**
cards.m: Antibiotics, inhalers and itchy skin never stop a jab.

cards.q: Which family, feeding and nutritional situations are NOT contraindications to vaccination?
cards.a:
• The **child's mother is pregnant**
• The child is **breastfed** (does not affect polio vaccine uptake)
• **Neonatal jaundice**
• **Underweight or malnourished** (these children need protection most)
cards.m: Malnourished children are the ones measles kills: vaccinate them first.

cards.q: A child is older than the recommended age, or the mother says the child already 'had measles'. Should you still vaccinate?
cards.a:
• **Over the recommended age**: not a contraindication; give catch-up doses
• **Past history of pertussis, measles or rubella**: vaccinate **unless the illness was medically confirmed**
• Parental recall of a rash is unreliable, and extra doses are harmless
cards.m: 'Had measles' without lab proof = has not had measles.

cards.q: Which neurological and cardiac histories are NOT contraindications to vaccination?
cards.a:
• **Stable neurological conditions**: cerebral palsy, intellectual disability, **febrile convulsions**, **stable epilepsy**
• **Family history of convulsions**
• **Heart disease**, congenital or acquired
• Note: slide uses the outdated term 'mental retardation'; use **intellectual disability**
• An evolving or unstable neurological condition is a reason to discuss with a specialist first
cards.m: Stable brain, family fits, sick heart: still vaccinate.

cards.q: How should a preterm baby be immunised?
cards.a:
• According to the schedule by **chronological age**, irrespective of gestational age
• **Do not correct** for prematurity and do not reduce doses
• Preterm babies are at **higher risk** of vaccine-preventable infections, so delay is harmful
• Prematurity is a **false contraindication**
cards.m: Born early, vaccinated on time.

cards.q: What are the rules on intervals between doses when catching up missed vaccines?
cards.a:
• Vaccines may be given with **shorter intervals** than the routine schedule to catch up
• **Minimum interval** between two doses of the **same vaccine** is **4 weeks**
• An interrupted series is **continued, never restarted**
cards.m: Catch up, do not start over; but never closer than 4 weeks.

cards.q: A child arrives at the clinic with no vaccination record. How is the child managed?
cards.a:
• A child with **unknown status or no documentation** is treated as having **never been immunised**
• Start an age-appropriate **catch-up schedule**
• Extra doses in a previously vaccinated child are not harmful
cards.m: No record, no vaccine.

cards.q: What is the minimum age for MMR in the Malaysian programme, and which vaccine gets priority in catch-up?
cards.a:
• MMR can only be given once the child reaches **9 months** of age (maternal antibodies interfere earlier)
• In catch-up, give priority to vaccines against **highly transmissible diseases** such as **measles (MMR/MR)**
• Then diphtheria-containing vaccines (DTaP-IPV//Hib, DT or Tdap)
cards.m: Measles first: it is the most contagious disease known (R0 12-18).

cards.q: How should several vaccines be given at the same visit?
cards.a:
• Two or more vaccines **can be given at the same time**, at **different injection sites**
• Example from the guideline: **BCG left arm**, **MMR/MR right arm**, **DTaP-IPV//Hib right thigh**, **Hepatitis B left thigh**
• **Document** each vaccine against its injection site
cards.m: One vaccine, one site, one record.

cards.q: Can two different live vaccines (e.g., MMR and varicella) be given on different days?
cards.a:
• Give live injectable vaccines **on the same day**, or separate them by **at least 4 weeks**
• If given a few days apart, the immune response to the first may **blunt the second**
• Inactivated vaccines can be given at any interval
cards.m: Live + live: same day or wait a month.

cards.q: Outline the infant and toddler part of the Malaysian National Immunisation Programme.
cards.a:
• **Birth**: BCG, Hepatitis B dose 1
• **2, 3, 5 months**: DTaP-IPV-Hib-HepB (hexavalent)
• **4 and 6 months**: pneumococcal (PCV), booster at **15 months**
• **9 and 12 months**: MMR
• **18 months**: DTaP-IPV/Hib booster
• Regional extras: measles at 6 months (Sabah), Japanese encephalitis (Sarawak)
• Check the current MOH schedule table (slide p38 is image only)
cards.m: Birth 2, then 2-3-5 for the six-in-one, 4-6-15 for pneumococcus, 9-12 for MMR, 18 to boost.

cards.q: Which vaccines are given at school age in the Malaysian programme?
cards.a:
• **7 years (Year 1)**: **DT** booster (and MR where scheduled)
• **Girls around 13 years** (school programme): **HPV**, 2 doses
• **15 years**: **tetanus** booster
• School health teams deliver these; check the record for missed infant doses at the same time
cards.m: 7 = DT, 13 = HPV, 15 = tetanus.

cards.q: What should parents know about BCG vaccination?
cards.a:
• Given at **birth**, intradermally over the **left deltoid**
• A small papule that **ulcerates and heals with a scar** over 6-12 weeks is **normal**: keep clean and dry, do not apply ointment
• **No repeat** BCG is needed if no scar develops
• **Live** vaccine: avoid in severe immunodeficiency (e.g., symptomatic HIV)
cards.m: BCG sore = normal; BCG scar missing = still no repeat.

cards.q: Is egg allergy a contraindication to MMR?
cards.a:
• **No**: MMR is grown in chick embryo fibroblast culture and contains negligible egg protein
• Children with egg allergy, even severe, can receive MMR in the usual clinic setting
• True contraindication is **anaphylaxis to a previous MMR dose** or a component (e.g., **neomycin, gelatin**)
cards.m: MMR is not an egg vaccine.

cards.q: A child is on high-dose oral prednisolone. When can live vaccines be given?
cards.a:
• High dose: about **≥ 2 mg/kg/day** (or ≥ 20 mg/day) for **≥ 14 days**
• **Defer live vaccines** until **at least 1 month after stopping** (some guidelines, e.g., UK Green Book, advise 3 months)
• Short courses, low doses, inhaled or topical steroids: **no delay**
• Inactivated vaccines can be given
cards.m: Big steroid dose for 2 weeks = wait a month for live vaccines.

cards.q: Should the healthy siblings of a child receiving chemotherapy be given MMR?
cards.a:
• **Yes**: vaccinating household contacts **protects** the immunosuppressed child (cocooning)
• MMR virus is **not transmitted** from vaccinated people
• Varicella vaccine is also recommended; avoid close contact only if the sibling develops a vaccine rash
• **Oral polio vaccine** should be avoided in contacts (Malaysia's schedule uses inactivated **IPV**)
• Household contacts should also have annual influenza vaccine
cards.m: Protect the fragile child by vaccinating everyone around them.

cards.q: What is the immunisation plan for a baby born to an HBsAg-positive mother?
cards.a:
• **Hepatitis B vaccine** at birth, ideally **within 12-24 hours**
• Plus **hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG)** at a different site, ideally within 12 hours
• Complete the infant series on schedule
• Test the infant for **HBsAg and anti-HBs** after completing the series (around 9-12 months)
• **Breastfeeding is allowed**
cards.m: Hep B-positive mother: two jabs at birth (vaccine + HBIG), two thighs.

cards.q: How do you immunise a child who has their first clinic visit late and has had no vaccines?
cards.a:
• Give **all vaccines due for age** at the first visit, at separate sites
• Prioritise **MMR/measles** if ≥ 9 months
• Then follow **minimum intervals** (4 weeks between doses of the same vaccine) to complete the series
• Fewer **Hib** and **pneumococcal** doses are needed the older the child is at the start (Hib not routinely needed after 5 years)
• Use the Paediatric Protocols catch-up tables (slides p42-43)
cards.m: Late starters: everything due today, then the shortest safe gaps.

cards.q: What is growth faltering?
cards.a:
• Previously called **failure to thrive**
• Children who **do not reach their expected weight, length or BMI for age**
• It is a **description, not a diagnosis**: look for organic and non-organic causes
• Judged by the **trend over serial measurements**, not a single point
cards.m: Growth faltering is a sign, like fever: find the cause.

cards.q: What practical centile thresholds suggest growth faltering in infants and young children?
cards.a:
• Weight falls across **≥ 2 major centile lines** (if birth weight was between the 9th and 91st centile)
• Fall across **1 centile space** if birth weight was **below the 9th** centile; 3 or more if above the 91st
• Current weight **below the 2nd centile**
• Note: some **centile crossing in the first 6-8 weeks** is normal as babies settle to their genetic track
cards.m: Two lines down = look around.

cards.q: How are underweight, stunting and wasting defined on WHO growth standards?
cards.a:
• **Underweight**: weight-for-age **< -2 SD** (z-score)
• **Stunting**: length/height-for-age **< -2 SD** (chronic undernutrition)
• **Wasting**: weight-for-length/height **< -2 SD** (acute undernutrition)
• **Severe** forms: **< -3 SD**
• Malaysia uses the **WHO Growth Standard 2006** charts
cards.m: Stunting = Short (chronic); Wasting = Thin (acute).

cards.q: What are the organic causes of growth faltering?
cards.a:
• **Malabsorption** (e.g., coeliac disease, cystic fibrosis, cow's milk protein allergy)
• **Chronic inflammatory disorders** (IBD, juvenile arthritis)
• **Chronic systemic disease**: cardiac, respiratory, renal, liver
• **Neurodevelopmental disorders** (e.g., cerebral palsy with feeding difficulty)
• **Genetic** conditions: Turner, Noonan syndrome
• **Endocrine**: hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency
cards.m: Organic causes: 'Gut, Heart, Lungs, Kidney, Liver, Brain, Genes, Glands'.

cards.q: What are the non-organic causes of growth faltering?
cards.a:
• **Inadequate calorie/nutrient intake**, limited food variety
• **Behavioural feeding difficulties**, poor parental feeding style
• Poor hygiene, **unhealthy sleep habits**
• **Psychosocial stress**, **neglect/abuse**
• **Economic/social deprivation**
• Non-organic causes are the **most common** in primary care
cards.m: Most faltering is about the plate and the home, not the organs.

cards.q: Why does Malaysia use the WHO Growth Standard 2006 charts?
cards.a:
• Built from healthy, **breastfed** children raised in optimal conditions in six countries
• Describes how children **should** grow (a standard), not just how they do grow (a reference)
• Used for anthropometric assessment in KK and in the Child Health Record Book
• Formula-fed babies may look 'heavier' on these charts; breastfed babies should not be labelled as faltering because of older reference charts
cards.m: WHO 2006 = the breastfed baby is the gold standard.

cards.q: What should a detailed milk-feeding history cover in a child with growth faltering?
cards.a:
• **Formula dilution ratio** and preparation method (over-dilution is common)
• **Volume per bottle**, number of bottles per day
• Duration and frequency of remaining **breastfeeds**
• **Fluid intake**: plain water, sweetened drinks or juice that **displace calorie-dense foods**
cards.m: Ask how many scoops, how much water, how many bottles.

cards.q: What should be asked about complementary feeding and the mealtime environment?
cards.a:
• **Age at introduction** of solids (around 6 months)
• **Texture progression** (purees to lumpy to family food)
• **Feeding frequency**
• Specific **food refusal / spitting**
• Mealtime **duration**, **coercion**, **distraction** (screens) and **parental stress** during feeds
cards.m: What, when, how lumpy, how long, how stressful.

cards.q: Which gastrointestinal causes should be explored through the bowel history in a child with growth faltering?
cards.a:
• Frequency, consistency, **blood or mucus**, **greasy/foul-smelling stools** (steatorrhoea)
• Consider **toddler's diarrhoea** (thriving child, undigested food in stool)
• **Post-enteritis secondary lactose intolerance**
• **Cow's milk protein allergy** (blood/mucus, eczema, vomiting)
• Vomiting: frequency, forcefulness, relation to feeds
cards.m: Greasy = malabsorption; bloody = allergy or infection; peas and carrots = toddler's diarrhoea.

cards.q: Which red flag symptoms in a child with growth faltering suggest an organic cause?
cards.a:
• **Recurrent fevers**
• **Chronic cough**
• **Lethargy**
• **Frequent infections** (respiratory or urinary)
• Also: chronic diarrhoea with steatorrhoea, persistent vomiting, developmental regression
cards.m: Fever, cough, tired, infections: the body is burning calories or losing them.

cards.q: What caregiver and psychosocial factors should be explored in growth faltering?
cards.a:
• **Caregiver transition**: mother returning to full-time work, change of primary carer (e.g., nursery, grandparent)
• Caregiver **feeding practices** and understanding of formula preparation and complementary feeding
• **Maternal postpartum well-being** (postnatal depression)
• **Financial and food security**
• **Caregiver-infant attachment**
cards.m: Who feeds the child, how well they cope, and whether there is food at home.

cards.q: Which developmental and past medical history items matter in growth faltering?
cards.a:
• Development across all domains to rule out **global developmental delay or regression**
• **Antenatal course** and **birth weight** (SGA, prematurity)
• **Neonatal screening**: **cord TSH** and **G6PD** results
• **Hospitalisations**
• **Vaccination status**
cards.m: Check the Buku Pink: birth weight, TSH, G6PD, vaccines, milestones.

cards.q: What are the key points in the general and anthropometric examination of a child with growth faltering?
cards.a:
• General: activity, interaction, **hydration**, **pallor**, **muscle wasting**/loss of subcutaneous fat, **oedema**, **dysmorphism**
• Measure **weight**, **recumbent length** (under 2 years) and **head circumference**
• Plot **serial** measurements; assess weight-for-age, length-for-age and weight-for-length
• Look at the **trend**, not one reading
• Examine mouth (thrush, cleft, tongue tie, dentition) and **observe an actual feed**
cards.m: Measure, plot, compare, and watch the child eat.

cards.q: What do different patterns of weight, length and head circumference suggest in a small child?
cards.a:
• **Weight falls first**, length later, head spared: **nutritional** (intake or absorption)
• Weight and length **both low and proportionate**, normal velocity: **familial/constitutional** short stature
• **Length falls more than weight** (child relatively overweight): **endocrine** (hypothyroidism, GH deficiency)
• **Small head circumference** with delay: **neurological/genetic** or congenital infection
cards.m: Weight drops first = food; height drops first = hormones; head drops first = brain.

cards.q: Which systemic examination findings point to an organic cause of growth faltering?
cards.a:
• **Cardiovascular**: murmur, tachycardia, signs of heart failure
• **Respiratory**: tachypnoea, chronic lung disease, clubbing
• **Abdominal**: distension, hepatosplenomegaly, masses
• **Neurological**: tone, power, developmental status
• **Skin/hair** changes of nutritional deficiency
cards.m: Head-to-toe for hidden calorie burners.

cards.q: Which baseline investigations are used selectively in growth faltering?
cards.a:
• **FBC ± serum ferritin**: anaemia/iron deficiency, especially with poor complementary feeding
• **Renal profile, electrolytes, LFT, albumin**: significant malnutrition, dehydration, suspected renal/hepatic disease
• **Urinalysis ± urine culture**: occult or recurrent **UTI**
• Investigations are **guided by history and examination**, not a blanket screen
cards.m: Selective, not shotgun.

cards.q: When are stool tests, malabsorption tests, thyroid function and CXR/echo indicated in growth faltering?
cards.a:
• **Stool examination ± culture**: persistent diarrhoea, blood/mucus, suspected infection
• **Malabsorption workup** (e.g., coeliac serology, stool fat): chronic diarrhoea, **steatorrhoea**
• **Thyroid function**: **poor linear growth** or features of hypothyroidism
• **CXR / echocardiography**: suspected cardiac, respiratory or other chronic disease
cards.m: Test what the story points to.

cards.q: What is the primary-care management of growth faltering?
cards.a:
• **Treat the underlying cause** (medical or feeding)
• **Optimise nutrition**: continue **breastfeeding**, optimise feed frequency; for formula-fed infants optimise **volume and frequency**; increase **calorie density** when appropriate; vitamins/minerals if indicated; **gluten-free diet** if coeliac disease confirmed
• **Refer to a dietitian** for individualised advice
• **Monitor** catch-up growth with regular follow-up
• Refer to paediatrics if organic cause suspected, no response, or safeguarding concerns
cards.m: Cause, Calories, Counsellor (dietitian), Chart again.

cards.q: What is Down syndrome and how is the diagnosis confirmed?
cards.a:
• Trisomy 21: the **most common chromosomal cause of intellectual disability**
• Distinct pattern of features affecting multiple systems
• Diagnosis: **clinical features** plus **chromosomal analysis (karyotype)**, prenatally or postnatally
• Note: slide p53 also shows the ADHD definition (copy-paste error); it does not apply to Down syndrome
cards.m: Suspect by face, prove by karyotype.

cards.q: What are the genetic mechanisms of Down syndrome and why does it matter which one?
cards.a:
• **Non-disjunction** (free trisomy 21): about **95%**, risk rises with **maternal age**
• **Robertsonian translocation**: about **4%**; one parent may be a balanced carrier
• **Mosaicism**: about **1%**, often milder phenotype
• Translocation found: **karyotype both parents**, because **recurrence risk is much higher** if a parent carries it
cards.m: 95-4-1: Non-disjunction, Translocation, Mosaic.

cards.q: What are the characteristic features of Down syndrome in a newborn?
cards.a:
• **Hypotonia** and **feeding difficulties**
• **Flat facial profile**, **flat nasal bridge**, **upslanting palpebral fissures**, **epicanthic folds**
• Small ears, protruding tongue, excess nuchal skin
• **Single palmar crease**, clinodactyly, **sandal gap**
• Brushfield spots on the iris
cards.m: Floppy baby, flat face, up-slanting eyes, single crease, sandal gap.

cards.q: What proportion of babies with Down syndrome have congenital heart disease, and which lesion is most typical?
cards.a:
• About **50%** have congenital heart disease
• **AVSD** (atrioventricular septal defect) is the most characteristic; also **VSD**, **ASD**, PDA, tetralogy of Fallot
• AVSD may have **no murmur** at birth because pulmonary pressures are still high
• Hence **echocardiography for every baby**, regardless of examination
cards.m: Half have a heart lesion; AVSD is the Down syndrome signature, and it can be silent.

cards.q: Which gastrointestinal anomalies are associated with Down syndrome and how do they present?
cards.a:
• Present in about **12%**
• **Duodenal atresia**: **bilious vomiting** in the first day(s), **double bubble** on abdominal X-ray (antenatal polyhydramnios)
• **Hirschsprung disease**: **delayed meconium** (> 48 h), abdominal distension, constipation, risk of enterocolitis
• Also anorectal malformations, coeliac disease later
cards.m: Down syndrome gut: 'double bubble' at the top, 'no poo' at the bottom.

cards.q: Which haematological, endocrine and eye problems should be looked for in a newborn with Down syndrome?
cards.a:
• **Transient abnormal myelopoiesis (TAM)**: blast cells on FBC in about 10%; usually resolves, but raises later **leukaemia** risk
• **Congenital hypothyroidism**
• **Congenital cataract**: check the **red reflex**
• Polycythaemia is also common
cards.m: Newborn Down syndrome checklist: Blood (FBC), Thyroid (TSH), Eyes (red reflex), Heart (echo).

cards.q: What medical problems develop in infancy and childhood in Down syndrome?
cards.a:
• **Developmental delay** and **intellectual disability**
• **Hearing loss** (glue ear, sensorineural) and **visual problems** (refractive errors, strabismus, cataract, keratoconus)
• **Recurrent respiratory infections** and **obstructive sleep apnoea**
• **Hypothyroidism** and **short stature**
• **Leukaemia**
• **Atlantoaxial instability**
cards.m: Ears, Eyes, Airway, Thyroid, Blood, Neck: the childhood watch list.

cards.q: What is atlantoaxial instability in Down syndrome and how is it monitored?
cards.a:
• Ligamentous laxity of C1-C2 can allow **spinal cord compression**
• Warning symptoms: **neck pain or torticollis**, change in gait, **loss of bladder/bowel control**, new clumsiness, weakness, **brisk reflexes**
• Routine screening X-rays in **asymptomatic** children are **no longer recommended**
• Symptoms: **urgent** neck imaging and referral; take care with neck positioning during anaesthesia
cards.m: Watch the neck by asking about the legs and bladder.

cards.q: What is the leukaemia risk in Down syndrome?
cards.a:
• Overall risk of leukaemia is about **10-20 times** higher than other children
• **AML (megakaryoblastic, M7)**: in early childhood, often preceded by **TAM**
• **ALL**: also increased
• Unexplained **pallor, bruising, bone pain, persistent fever** or hepatosplenomegaly: urgent **FBC** and referral
cards.m: TAM in the newborn is a warning flag for AML before age 4.

cards.q: What problems occur in adolescence and adulthood in Down syndrome?
cards.a:
• **Females often fertile**; **males usually infertile**
• **Anxiety and depression**
• **Thyroid** and other **autoimmune** disorders (coeliac, diabetes, alopecia)
• Greatly increased risk of **early-onset Alzheimer's disease** (amyloid precursor protein gene on chromosome 21)
• **Reduced life expectancy** (now around 60 years)
cards.m: Chromosome 21 carries the APP gene, so an extra copy means extra amyloid and earlier dementia.

cards.q: What are the baseline investigations after a baby is diagnosed with Down syndrome?
cards.a:
• **Chromosomal analysis** (karyotype) to confirm and identify the type
• **FBC** (TAM, polycythaemia)
• **T4/TSH** at birth or at **1-2 weeks**
• **Echocardiogram by 6 weeks** of age (earlier if abnormal findings)
• Plus newborn **hearing screen** and **red reflex**
cards.m: Karyotype, Count, Thyroid, Echo: KCTE before 6 weeks.

cards.q: Beyond tests, what does early management of a child with Down syndrome involve?
cards.a:
• **Early intervention**: physiotherapy, **speech therapy**, developmental programmes started early
• **Family counselling and support**: genetic counselling, assess family needs, link to **support groups**
• **Breastfeeding support** (hypotonia makes feeding hard)
• Register for regular **health surveillance**
cards.m: Therapy early, family supported, surveillance for life.

cards.q: What ongoing health surveillance does a child with Down syndrome need?
cards.a:
• **Thyroid function** at least **yearly**
• **Hearing** assessment regularly (about yearly in childhood)
• **Eye/vision** checks (refraction, cataract, keratoconus)
• **Growth** on **Down syndrome-specific charts**
• Ask about **snoring/sleep apnoea** and neck symptoms
• Development, behaviour, dental care and immunisations (standard schedule)
cards.m: Annual TEA: Thyroid, Ears, And eyes, plus sleep and neck questions.

cards.q: How do you counsel parents of a child with Down syndrome about recurrence risk?
cards.a:
• **Free trisomy 21**: recurrence about **1%**, or the maternal-age risk if higher
• **Translocation** with a **carrier parent**: much higher, especially if the **mother** is the carrier (around 10-15%)
• **Rare 21;21 translocation** carrier: nearly 100%
• Offer **genetic counselling** and **prenatal screening/diagnosis** in future pregnancies
cards.m: Free trisomy = about 1%; parent carries the translocation = much higher.

cards.q: How is ADHD defined?
cards.a:
• A **persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity**
• **More frequent and severe** than typically seen at that child's **developmental stage**
• Neurodevelopmental disorder, starts in childhood
• Diagnosed by **DSM-5** criteria or ICD-10 hyperkinetic disorder
cards.m: ADHD = more than normal for age, in more than one place, for more than a moment.

cards.q: What are the biological risk factors for ADHD?
cards.a:
• **Male sex** (boys diagnosed about 2-3 times more often)
• **Genetics**: increased risk in relatives of people with ADHD (highly heritable)
• Perinatal biology: **preterm birth**, **low birth weight**, **low APGAR score**
cards.m: Boys, genes, born early.

cards.q: Which pre-pregnancy and prenatal factors increase the risk of ADHD?
cards.a:
• Pre-pregnancy **maternal obesity**
• **Hypertensive disorders** of pregnancy, **maternal diabetes**
• **Maternal psychosocial stress**
• Maternal **cigarette, drug and alcohol** use
• Maternal **paracetamol** use and **valproate** use
cards.m: Prenatal 'SODA-VP': Smoking/substances, Obesity, Diabetes, Alcohol, Valproate, Paracetamol (plus hypertension and stress).

cards.q: Which childhood factors are listed as ADHD risk factors?
cards.a:
• **Traumatic brain injury**
• **Nutritional factors**
• **Screen time > 2 hours/day**
• Advise families to limit recreational screen time as part of management
cards.m: Head injury, poor diet, too much screen.

cards.q: What are the DSM-5 diagnostic thresholds for ADHD?
cards.a:
• **≥ 6 symptoms** of inattention and/or **≥ 6** of hyperactivity-impulsivity (**≥ 5** if aged **17 or older**)
• Present for **≥ 6 months**
• Several symptoms present **before age 12**
• Present in **≥ 2 settings** (e.g., home and school)
• Clear **functional impairment**; not better explained by another disorder
cards.m: 6-6-12-2: six symptoms, six months, before twelve, two settings.

cards.q: Give typical inattention symptoms of ADHD.
cards.a:
• Careless mistakes, poor attention to detail
• Difficulty **sustaining attention** in tasks or play
• Does not seem to **listen** when spoken to
• Fails to **finish** schoolwork or chores
• Poor **organisation**; avoids tasks needing sustained mental effort
• **Loses things**, easily **distracted**, **forgetful** in daily activities
cards.m: The inattentive child is the daydreamer who loses the pencil and never finishes the worksheet.

cards.q: Give typical hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms of ADHD.
cards.a:
• **Fidgets**, squirms, leaves seat when expected to stay seated
• Runs or climbs inappropriately; always 'on the go'
• Cannot play quietly; **talks excessively**
• **Blurts out answers**, **cannot wait** for a turn
• **Interrupts** or intrudes on others
cards.m: Motor that will not switch off and a mouth that will not wait.

cards.q: What are the three presentations of ADHD, and why are girls often missed?
cards.a:
• **Predominantly inattentive**
• **Predominantly hyperactive-impulsive**
• **Combined** (most common in clinic)
• Girls more often have the **inattentive** type: quiet, daydreaming, under-achieving, so they are referred **later** or labelled lazy
cards.m: Boys disrupt the class; girls drift out of it.

cards.q: What should the history cover in a child referred with possible ADHD?
cards.a:
• **Core symptoms**: inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity
• **Behaviour in school** and **academic performance** (teacher report)
• **Age of onset**, duration and progression
• **Activities of daily living** functioning
• Restless, fidgety, disruptive and **unsafe behaviour** (injuries)
• Plus sleep, family history, psychosocial stressors
cards.m: Onset, Settings, School, Safety, Sleep.

cards.q: Why is physical examination and mental state examination important before diagnosing ADHD?
cards.a:
• Physical: **vital signs**, **height and weight** (baseline for stimulants), hearing and vision, dysmorphism, neurocutaneous signs
• Excludes **mimics**: hearing/visual impairment, **hypothyroidism**, **absence seizures**, **obstructive sleep apnoea**, iron deficiency, medication effects
• MSE: appearance, activity, social interaction, speech and language, mood, thought, **attention**, intelligence and academic skills
cards.m: Before you call it ADHD, make sure the child can hear, see, sleep and is not seizing.

cards.q: Which behavioural rating scales are used in ADHD assessment?
cards.a:
• **Conners' Rating Scales (CRS)**
• **Vanderbilt ADHD Rating Scale**
• **ADHD Rating Scale-5**
• **Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL)**
• **Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ)**
• Collect from **both parent and teacher** to show pervasiveness; scales support but **do not make** the diagnosis
cards.m: Conners and Vanderbilt: one form for home, one for school.

cards.q: According to the MOH CPG, what must be true of the core symptoms for an ADHD diagnosis?
cards.a:
• **Persistent**
• **Pervasive**: present in **2 or more settings**
• Cause **significant functional impairment**
• **Not better accounted for** by another mental disorder (e.g., ASD/pervasive developmental disorder, psychosis, **depression**, **anxiety**)
cards.m: Persistent, Pervasive, Problematic, and not Pretenders.

cards.q: What are the common comorbidities of ADHD?
cards.a:
• **Learning disorders**
• **Sleep disorders**
• **Oppositional defiant disorder (ODD)**
• **Conduct disorder**
• **Chronic tic disorder**
• Screen for these, as they change management and prognosis
cards.m: ADHD rarely travels alone: Learning, Sleep, ODD, Conduct, Tics.

cards.q: When is medication offered for ADHD and what are the main drugs?
cards.a:
• Offered to children **aged 6 years and above** and adolescents (with ongoing non-drug measures)
• **Methylphenidate**: **stimulant**, first-line
• **Atomoxetine**: **non-stimulant**, alternative (e.g., stimulant not tolerated, tics, substance-misuse risk)
• Under 6 years: **parent training/behavioural therapy first**; drugs only by specialists
cards.m: Under 6: train the parents. Over 6: add methylphenidate.

cards.q: What are the side effects of methylphenidate and what must be monitored?
cards.a:
• **Reduced appetite**, weight loss, **insomnia**, headache, abdominal pain
• Raised **heart rate and blood pressure**
• May worsen **tics** or anxiety; possible **growth slowing**
• Before starting: cardiac history and examination, baseline **height, weight, HR, BP**
• Monitor these regularly; give after breakfast; consider drug holidays
cards.m: Stimulant steals Sleep, Supper and Stature, and speeds the heart.

cards.q: What non-pharmacological interventions are used in ADHD?
cards.a:
• **Psychoeducation** for child, family and teachers
• **Family-based** (parent training) and **school-based** interventions (classroom strategies, seating, short tasks)
• **Organisational skills training**
• Psychological: **CBT-based** and **mindfulness-based** interventions
• **Occupational therapy** (adjunct), **assistive technology**
cards.m: Teach the family, tune the classroom, train organisation.

cards.q: How is autism spectrum disorder defined?
cards.a:
• A **neurodevelopmental disorder**
• Impairments in **communication**, **social functioning** and **behaviour**
• **Begins in early childhood**
• A spectrum: severity and intellectual ability vary widely
cards.m: ASD = Social, Speech and Sameness.

cards.q: What are the DSM-5 core criteria for autism spectrum disorder?
cards.a:
• **A. Persistent deficits in social communication and interaction**: social-emotional reciprocity, non-verbal communication (eye contact, gestures), developing and maintaining relationships
• **B. Restricted, repetitive behaviours/interests** (≥ 2): stereotyped movements or speech (echolalia, hand-flapping), **insistence on sameness**, fixated interests, **sensory hyper- or hypo-reactivity**
• Present in the **early developmental period**, cause impairment, not better explained by intellectual disability
cards.m: Two pillars: Social communication + Repetitive/restricted behaviour.

cards.q: What are the risk factors for autism spectrum disorder?
cards.a:
• **Maternal age > 40** years; **paternal age > 50** years
• **First-born** of mother > 35 and father > 40
• **Prematurity < 33 weeks**
• **Neonatal encephalopathy**
• **Family history** of ASD (siblings have markedly higher risk)
cards.m: Older parents, very early birth, brain injury at birth, autistic sibling.

cards.q: What are the early red flags for autism spectrum disorder?
cards.a:
• **No babbling or pointing** (or other gestures) by **12 months**
• Poor **eye contact**, does not **respond to name**
• Lack of **joint attention** (does not show or share interest)
• **No single words by 16 months**; **no spontaneous 2-word phrases by 24 months**
• **Any loss of language or social skills** at any age
cards.m: 12-16-24 rule: gestures by 12, words by 16, phrases by 24.

cards.q: What is the M-CHAT and when is it used?
cards.a:
• **Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers**
• **23-item** questionnaire on behaviour and development, completed by **parents**
• Recommended at **18 months** (early identification) and **24 months** (to identify toddlers who **regress**)
• A screening tool: a positive screen needs **follow-up and referral**, not a diagnosis
cards.m: M-CHAT: parents answer, the doctor follows up.

cards.q: How is the M-CHAT-R/F (revised version) scored?
cards.a:
• **20 items**, yes/no
• **0-2: low risk**, rescreen at 24 months if under 2 years
• **3-7: medium risk**: do the **Follow-up interview**; if still **≥ 2**, refer
• **8-20: high risk**: **refer immediately** for diagnostic evaluation and early intervention
• (The original 23-item M-CHAT used failure of ≥ 3 items or ≥ 2 critical items)
cards.m: Under 3 = relax, 3-7 = recheck, 8+ = refer.

cards.q: What is the Social Communication Questionnaire (SCQ)?
cards.a:
• **Parent-rated** questionnaire for ASD screening
• For children **older than 4 years**
• **Better at detection** in those **older than 7 years**
• Used when the child is too old for the M-CHAT
cards.m: M-CHAT for toddlers, SCQ for school-age children.

cards.q: What should the history cover in a child with suspected autism?
cards.a:
• **Parental concerns** and symptoms suspicious of ASD
• **Developmental history** (including regression)
• Behaviour and **interaction with others**
• **Prenatal and perinatal** history; medical history
• **Psychiatric history** (co-existing mental disorders)
• **Family**, social, medication and allergy history
cards.m: Take the whole developmental story, from womb to now.

cards.q: What should you look for on physical examination of a child with suspected autism?
cards.a:
• **Dysmorphic features** and **congenital anomalies** (e.g., fragile X)
• Stigmata of **neurofibromatosis** (café-au-lait spots) or **tuberous sclerosis** (ash-leaf macules; use Wood's lamp)
• Speech/communication and developmental assessment
• **Hearing and vision** assessment
• Signs of **physical abuse or self-harm**
• Head circumference
cards.m: Look at the face, the skin and the scars.

cards.q: Which tools are used to diagnose autism spectrum disorder?
cards.a:
• **ADI-R**: Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised (parent interview)
• **ADOS**: Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (observing the child)
• **DISCO**: Diagnostic Interview for Social and Communication Disorders
• **CARS**: Childhood Autism Rating Scale
• Used by trained specialists (CDC, developmental paediatrician), alongside DSM-5 criteria
cards.m: Screen with M-CHAT; diagnose with ADOS/ADI-R.

cards.q: What is the one routine investigation for every child with suspected ASD, and why?
cards.a:
• **Audiological (hearing) test**
• **Hearing impairment** can mimic ASD: poor response to name, delayed speech, social withdrawal
• Further tests (genetic, EEG) only if clinically indicated (dysmorphism, seizures, regression)
cards.m: Before 'autism', rule out 'can't hear'.

cards.q: What are the common comorbidities of autism spectrum disorder?
cards.a:
• **Intellectual disability**
• **ADHD**
• **Sleep problems**
• **Epilepsy**
• **Gastrointestinal problems** (e.g., constipation)
• **Motor coordination deficits**
cards.m: ASD plus: IQ, ADHD, Sleep, Seizures, Stomach, Clumsiness.

cards.q: What are the non-pharmacological interventions for autism spectrum disorder?
cards.a:
• **Applied Behaviour Analysis (ABA)**
• **Speech, language and communication** intervention
• **Occupational therapy** (sensory, fine motor, self-care)
• **Social skills** and **self-help skills** training
• **Parent education and support** (parent-mediated intervention)
• **CBT** for older, verbally able children with anxiety
• These are the **mainstay**: start early
cards.m: Behaviour, Speech, OT, Social skills, Parents: therapy first, tablets second.

cards.q: What is the role of medication in autism spectrum disorder?
cards.a:
• **No drug treats the core** social-communication features
• **Atypical antipsychotic** (e.g., **risperidone**) for **short-term irritability**/aggression
• **Antidepressants** (SSRI, TCA) for co-existing anxiety/depression or repetitive behaviour
• **Methylphenidate / atomoxetine** for co-existing **hyperactivity**
• **Melatonin** for **sleep difficulty**
• Monitor weight and metabolic effects with risperidone
cards.m: Drugs target the add-ons: Rage (risperidone), Restlessness (methylphenidate), Rest (melatonin).

cards.q: Parents ask whether the MMR vaccine caused their son's autism. How do you respond?
cards.a:
• **No**: large population studies show **no link** between MMR (or any vaccine) and autism
• The 1998 study claiming a link was **fraudulent and retracted**; the author was struck off
• ASD signs often become noticeable around **12-18 months**, the same age MMR is given, so the timing is coincidental
• Continue the **immunisation schedule**, including for siblings
cards.m: Same age, not same cause.

cards.q: How do you tell autism from an isolated expressive language delay in a 2-year-old?
cards.a:
• **Language delay alone**: good **eye contact**, **points** and uses gestures to communicate, shares interest (**joint attention**), plays pretend, responds to name
• **ASD**: poor eye contact and joint attention, **no compensating gestures**, repetitive play, restricted interests, may have regression
• Both need a **hearing test** and speech therapy referral; ASD features need **CDC/paediatric** assessment
cards.m: A late talker still points and shares; an autistic child often does neither.

cards.q: What is dyslexia?
cards.a:
• A **neurodevelopmental** specific learning disorder
• Difficulty **reading** and **processing written language**
• Occurs despite **normal intelligence**, vision, hearing and adequate teaching
• Core problem: **phonological processing** (linking sounds to letters)
cards.m: Dys-lexia = difficulty with words (lexis).

cards.q: Which three reading skills are impaired in dyslexia?
cards.a:
• **Decoding**: sounding out words
• **Encoding**: spelling words
• **Fluency**: reading at a good pace without mistakes
cards.m: Dyslexia trips on DEF: Decoding, Encoding, Fluency.

cards.q: What are the early signs of dyslexia in young children?
cards.a:
• **Mispronouncing** words
• Struggling to learn **nursery rhymes** or rhyming song lyrics
• **Mixing up similar-looking letters** (e.g., **b and d**)
• Little interest in learning **letters and sounds**
• Slow, effortful reading and poor spelling once at school
cards.m: b-d reversal and no rhyme: think dyslexia.

cards.q: How is dyslexia managed?
cards.a:
• **Phonological intervention**: phonological awareness, alphabet knowledge, early decoding skills
• **Repeated oral reading** programme
• **Individual or small-group teaching**
• School support (e.g., MOE **Special Recovery Programme**), extra exam time
• Check vision and hearing; screen for co-existing ADHD
cards.m: Teach the sounds, read aloud again and again, in small groups.

cards.q: What is dyscalculia and how does it present?
cards.a:
• Impairment in **mathematics**: **number sense**, memorising **arithmetic facts**, **accurate calculation**, mathematical **reasoning**
• Difficulty with basic arithmetic operations
• Trouble understanding **number concepts**
• Difficulty with maths **problem-solving**
• May struggle with **telling time**, measurement and **spatial awareness**
cards.m: Dys-calculia = difficulty with calculating; clocks and money are often hard too.

cards.q: How is dyscalculia managed?
cards.a:
• **Intensive teaching** using a **variety of techniques**
• **Concrete materials** (blocks, counters, number lines)
• Repeated practice in **counting and number skills**
• Classroom accommodations (calculators, extra time)
cards.m: Make numbers touchable.

cards.q: What is dysgraphia?
cards.a:
• A learning disorder affecting **writing abilities**
• Difficulty with **handwriting**, **spelling** and/or **organising written work**
• Related to a nervous system problem affecting the **fine motor skills** needed to write
• **Not** due to lack of intelligence or motivation
cards.m: Dys-graphia = difficulty with graphics (writing).
