cards.q: How is dysgraphia managed?
cards.a:
• **Occupational therapy**: fine motor skills, pencil grip, letter formation
• **Physical therapy**: posture, shoulder and core stability
• Accommodations: typing/keyboard, extra time, reduced copying
cards.m: Writing problem = hand problem = OT.

cards.q: Dyslexia vs dyscalculia vs dysgraphia: what is the main deficit and main therapy in each?
cards.a:
• **Dyslexia**: **reading** (decoding, spelling, fluency) - **phonological intervention**, repeated oral reading
• **Dyscalculia**: **maths** (number sense, calculation, reasoning) - **intensive teaching with concrete materials**
• **Dysgraphia**: **writing** (handwriting, spelling, organisation; fine motor) - **occupational therapy**, physiotherapy
• All occur with **normal intelligence**
cards.m: Lexia = read, Calculia = count, Graphia = write.

cards.q: A 9-year-old has poor school performance. What should the KK doctor assess before suspecting a specific learning disorder?
cards.a:
• **Hearing and vision**
• **Intellectual disability** (global rather than specific difficulty)
• **ADHD** (rating scales from parent and teacher), **absence seizures**, sleep problems
• **Emotional and social** factors: bullying, family stress, abuse, depression
• School attendance and quality of teaching
• Then refer for psycho-educational assessment and school support
cards.m: Before blaming the brain, check the Eyes, Ears, Attention, Absences and the home.

cards.q: What is an early intervention programme?
cards.a:
• **Coordinated services** for young children aged **0-6 years** with developmental delays or disabilities
• **Tailored** to the child's developmental needs and the **family's needs**
• Aim: support development and **improve functional outcomes early**
cards.m: EIP = right help, right child, right now (0-6 years).

cards.q: Which therapies make up early intervention, and what is meant by a family-centred approach?
cards.a:
• Targeted therapies: **speech and language therapy**, **occupational therapy**, **physiotherapy**
• **Family-centred**: parents are **coached, supported and empowered** to take part in the child's development
• Parents carry out therapy activities at home every day
cards.m: The therapist sees the child weekly; the parent sees them daily.

cards.q: Why should a child who misses milestones not be managed with 'wait and see'?
cards.a:
• The early years are a period of **rapid brain development and plasticity**
• Early intervention gives the **right foundation** for teaching, training and supporting development
• Pathway: **early identification** leads to **early support**, which leads to **better developmental opportunities**
• Intervention can start **before a final diagnosis**
cards.m: The brain is most mouldable early: do not waste the window.

cards.q: What are the four core components of an effective early intervention programme?
cards.a:
• **Developmental foundations**: sensory, motor, cognitive development; coordination and problem-solving
• **Communication and social skills**: language, understanding social cues, expressing needs, social interaction
• **Emotional well-being and adaptive skills**: emotional regulation, self-care (feeding, dressing), independence
• **Early literacy skills**: print awareness, vocabulary, phonological awareness, narrative skills, school readiness
cards.m: Move, Talk, Feel and cope, Read: four building blocks.

cards.q: What is the role of the KKIA (Klinik Kesihatan Ibu dan Anak) in early intervention?
cards.a:
• The **primary-care gateway** for routine **milestone tracking** and **developmental screening**
• Tools: Child Development Assessment Guide, **M-CHAT**
• Children with flags are **channelled to hospital-based rehabilitation** and specialist services
• Also links families to community services (PDK)
cards.m: KKIA finds them; hospitals and communities help them.

cards.q: What do Child Development Centres (CDC) and hospital paediatric rehabilitation clinics provide?
cards.a:
• **CDC (Pusat Perkembangan Kanak-Kanak)**: tertiary units at major hospitals (e.g., Hospital Tunku Azizah, Hospital Selayang, HCTM)
• **Multidisciplinary diagnostic assessment** and clinical early intervention: developmental paediatrician, speech-language therapist, OT, physiotherapist, clinical psychologist
• **Hospital paediatric rehabilitation clinics**: outpatient **OT** (sensory integration, fine motor, ADL), **speech therapy** and **physiotherapy**
cards.m: CDC = diagnose and plan; rehab clinic = deliver the therapy.

cards.q: What is the Program Pemulihan Dalam Komuniti (PDK)?
cards.a:
• **Community-based rehabilitation (CBR)** run by **JKM** (Ministry of Women, Family and Community Development)
• Centres **nationwide** for toddlers and preschool children with disabilities
• Offers **early stimulation**, motor coordination, cognitive readiness and basic **self-care** skills
• Includes **home-based** rehabilitation support
• Useful where hospital therapy is far away or infrequent
cards.m: PDK = therapy in the community, by JKM, near home.

cards.q: What are Genius Kurnia and the Genius early intervention modules?
cards.a:
• **Genius Kurnia** (formerly **PERMATA Kurnia**): government-funded early intervention and preschool education for children with **ASD aged 2-6**, using **applied behavioural intervention** and **parent training**
• **Genius Memperkasa Remaja & Kanak-Kanak**: early intervention modules for young children with **developmental delays or socio-developmental risks**
cards.m: Kurnia = Kids with autism, 2-6.

cards.q: What special education support does the Ministry of Education (MOE) provide?
cards.a:
• **Special Recovery Programme** (for pupils with learning difficulties, e.g., dyslexia)
• **Special Education Integration Programme (PPKI)**: special classes in mainstream schools
• **Inclusive Education Programme**: pupils with special needs in mainstream classes
• **Special Education Service Centre (3PK)**
• For **Murid Berkeperluan Khas (MBPK)**: visual, hearing, speech, physical and learning disabilities
cards.m: Recovery, Integration (PPKI), Inclusion, Service centre (3PK).

cards.q: Why should parents of a child with a confirmed developmental disability be advised to register the child as OKU?
cards.a:
• Registration with **JKM** as **Orang Kurang Upaya (OKU)** after medical certification
• Gives access to **welfare assistance**, PDK, special education placement, therapy and transport benefits
• The doctor completes the **medical certification form**
cards.m: OKU card = key to the support system.

cards.q: How is child abuse defined, and what are its forms?
cards.a:
• WHO (1999): all forms of **physical** and/or **emotional ill-treatment**, **sexual abuse**, **neglect** or negligent treatment, or **commercial or other exploitation**
• Resulting in **actual or potential harm** to the child's health, survival, development or dignity
• In the context of a relationship of **responsibility, trust or power**
cards.m: Four plus one: Physical, Emotional, Sexual, Neglect, plus Exploitation.

cards.q: Who is a 'child' under Malaysian law?
cards.a:
• Anyone **below 18 years** of age
• Defined in the **Child Act 2001**
• So a 16- or 17-year-old adolescent is still covered by child protection procedures
cards.m: Under 18 = child, however grown-up they look.

cards.q: Which features of the history should raise suspicion of non-accidental injury?
cards.a:
• **Delay in seeking medical care**
• **No explanation**, a **vague or changing** explanation, or **inconsistent** stories between carers
• Mechanism **incompatible with the injury** or with the child's **developmental stage** (e.g., a 3-month-old 'rolled off the bed' with a femoral fracture)
• **Repeated injuries** or frequent attendances; carer's inappropriate affect
cards.m: The story does not fit the injury, the age or the clock.

cards.q: Which bruising patterns suggest physical abuse?
cards.a:
• **Any bruise in a non-mobile infant** ('those who don't cruise rarely bruise')
• **TEN-4**: bruising on **Torso, Ears, Neck** in a child under 4 years, or **any** bruise under 4 months
• Bruising on cheeks, eyelids, buttocks, genitalia, upper arms
• **Patterned** bruises: hand slap marks, loop (belt/cable) marks, grip marks, **bite marks**
• Multiple bruises of different ages; check platelets and clotting
cards.m: Accidental bruises are on bony fronts (shins, forehead); abusive ones are on soft, hidden places.

cards.q: Which fractures are highly specific for physical abuse in infants?
cards.a:
• **Posterior rib fractures** (squeezing of the chest)
• **Metaphyseal corner (bucket-handle) fractures** (shaking or pulling of limbs)
• **Multiple fractures of different ages**
• **Femoral or humeral fractures in a non-ambulant** child
• Complex skull fractures with a trivial history
• Hence **skeletal survey** in children **under 2 years**
cards.m: Back ribs and bucket handles = someone squeezed or shook.

cards.q: Which burn patterns suggest non-accidental injury?
cards.a:
• **Immersion scalds** with **sharp, uniform 'glove-and-stocking'** margins and no splash marks
• **Sparing of flexural creases** or the buttock centre (child held down in hot water)
• **Cigarette burns**: round, 5-10 mm, uniform depth
• **Contact burns** with the shape of an iron or heater
• Burns on the back, buttocks or perineum
cards.m: Accidental scalds splash; inflicted scalds have straight edges.

cards.q: What is the classic triad of abusive head trauma (shaken baby syndrome)?
cards.a:
• **Subdural haemorrhage**
• **Retinal haemorrhages** (often multilayered, extensive)
• **Encephalopathy** (lethargy, vomiting, seizures, apnoea, poor feeding)
• Often **no external injury**; posterior rib fractures may co-exist
• Investigation: **CT head**, **fundoscopy**, skeletal survey
cards.m: Shaken baby: blood around the brain, blood in the eyes, baby not right.

cards.q: What is the One Stop Crisis Centre (OSCC)?
cards.a:
• An **integrated, multiagency service centre** in **all Emergency and Trauma Departments** of government hospitals
• Manages survivors of **domestic violence, sexual assault, child abuse and neglect**
• Goals: identify and manage survivors, **multidisciplinary care**, **crisis intervention**, optimal care and **medico-legal evidence** management
cards.m: OSCC = one door in the ED for every survivor.

cards.q: What is the SCAN team, who is in it and what are its goals?
cards.a:
• **Suspected Child Abuse and Neglect** team: hospital-based, trained multidisciplinary team
• Members: **paediatricians**, **gynaecologists**, mental health professionals, A&E staff, **forensic pathologists**, nurses, **medical social workers**, plus **JKM welfare officers** and **police**
• Goals: **reduce trauma** to the child, improve **coordination**, ensure **forensic defensibility**, enhance the **courts' ability to protect** families
cards.m: SCAN = Specialists, Social workers, JKM and Police around one child.

cards.q: What are the MOH principles for medical officers managing suspected child abuse?
cards.a:
• **Understand the local procedures** (SCAN/OSCC pathway)
• **Never work alone** in managing or evaluating an abused child
• Examination and medical reports should be done by **specialists**, unless none is available (e.g., district hospitals)
• Avoid repeated examinations and interviews
cards.m: Not alone, not repeatedly, and by the specialist where possible.

cards.q: What is the legal duty of a doctor who suspects child abuse in Malaysia?
cards.a:
• **Child Act 2001, Section 27**: a medical officer or registered medical practitioner who believes on **reasonable grounds** that a child has been physically or emotionally injured by ill-treatment, neglect, abandonment or exposure, or **sexually abused**, must **immediately inform a Protector** (JKM social welfare officer)
• **Failure to notify is an offence**
• Proof is not required: **reasonable suspicion** is enough
• Notify via the SCAN team / JKM; involve police as appropriate
cards.m: Suspect, then report: the investigation is not your job, the notification is.

cards.q: What must be covered in the history and examination of suspected physical abuse?
cards.a:
• History: **timing and nature of injuries**, full **developmental history**, **social history**
• Exam (documented carefully, with body charts): **bruises and lacerations**, check **ears**, **oral cavity including the frenulum**, and **fundoscopy** for haemorrhage
• Assess **growth**, development, emotion, physical maturity, **personal hygiene** and signs of **neglect**
• **Examine siblings** at home as relevant; observe **child-carer interaction**
cards.m: Ears, mouth, eyes: the hidden places abuse leaves marks.

cards.q: Which investigations are done in suspected physical abuse?
cards.a:
• **Platelet count and coagulation screen** if there is bruising (exclude bleeding disorder)
• **Skeletal survey** in children **under 2 years**
• **Photographs** of injuries
• **CT head** for head injury / suspected shaken baby syndrome
• **Ultrasound abdomen** for intra-abdominal injury (free fluid, haematoma)
• **X-rays** of suspected fractures
cards.m: Clotting, Clicks (skeletal survey), Camera, CT.

cards.q: How should the history be taken in suspected child sexual abuse?
cards.a:
• Initial history from the **person who first brought the child**, plus background
• Children may be helped to talk using **play materials**
• Build **rapport**, use **open-ended questions** and a **non-judgemental** style
• **Interview the parent/carer separately** from the child
• Past injuries (especially genital); in adolescents ask about **menstrual history, previous sexual activity, contraception, pregnancy**
cards.m: Open, gentle, separate: never lead the child.

cards.q: What principles apply to the examination of a child for sexual abuse?
cards.a:
• **Child-oriented**, adequately equipped, **quiet, informal and private** setting
• **Explain** to the child the reason for the examination
• **Never use force**
• **Avoid repeated vaginal examinations**
• **Absence of physical findings never excludes sexual abuse** (most examinations are normal)
cards.m: Normal exam does not mean nothing happened.

cards.q: When is examination for child sexual abuse urgent, non-urgent, or under anaesthesia?
cards.a:
• **Urgent**: obvious or suspected internal **trauma**, **genital bleeding**, discharge or pain, systemic illness, **last incident within 72 hours** (forensic evidence may last only hours), extreme distress
• **Non-urgent**: last incident **> 72 hours**, usually **long-term abuse**; planned as part of SCAN evaluation, **disclosure interview first**
• **Under anaesthesia**: distraught child where exam is essential, **painful injuries** (e.g., vaginal wall tear), STI swabs impossible, suspected **foreign body**
• Primary care: only a **limited exam** to judge urgency, then refer for specialist examination
cards.m: 72 hours is the forensic clock.

cards.q: What prophylaxis is given after acute sexual assault of an adolescent (MOH 2009 guideline), and how has practice changed?
cards.a:
• Examination by **O&G** as soon as possible if **< 72 h**
• **Emergency contraception**: slide gives the Yuzpe method (**Microgynon 30**, 4 tablets stat and 4 tablets 12 h later); current preferred option is **levonorgestrel 1.5 mg single dose** (or ulipristal), as early as possible
• **STI antibiotics** for high-risk cases: slide lists **doxycycline 100 mg bd + metronidazole 200 mg tds** (current regimens also cover gonorrhoea, e.g., ceftriaxone)
• **HIV PEP** after counselling, within **72 h**, with ID input. Note: slide lists AZT 250 mg/lamivudine/indinavir (outdated); current PEP is e.g., **tenofovir + emtricitabine/lamivudine + dolutegravir for 28 days**
cards.m: After assault, think 'EC, STI, HIV' within 72 hours.

cards.q: What supportive, documentation and legal steps follow a sexual abuse case?
cards.a:
• **Documentation**: written immediately, factual, concise, in the **child's own words**, signed, named and dated
• **Refer to medical social worker** for all abuse/neglect cases
• **Psychiatric referral** if suicidal risk or depression (parents too if needed)
• Inform parents early about **JKM referral / police report**, after considering the child's safety and the abuser's identity
• **Court**: give documentation (with investigating officer's name) to police; doctor may give evidence
• **Follow-up** with paediatrician/psychiatrist/counsellor after discharge
cards.m: Document, Defend (safety), Discuss (MSW, family), Depose (court), Don't drop follow-up.

mcq.stem:
A 1-day-old term boy is seen at a postnatal home visit after a prolonged second stage ending in a vacuum delivery. The mother noticed his head 'getting bigger' over the morning. There is a soft, fluctuant, boggy swelling extending from the forehead to the nape of the neck and across the suture lines. He is pale, HR 182/min, capillary refill 4 seconds.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Caput succedaneum
Cephalohaematoma of the parietal bone
Subaponeurotic haemorrhage
Chignon from the vacuum cup
Occipital encephalocele
mcq.e: A boggy swelling that spreads across sutures and grows after birth, with signs of hypovolaemia, is a subaponeurotic (subgaleal) haemorrhage. The subaponeurotic space is large and unconfined, so a newborn can lose a large share of blood volume into it. Caput also crosses sutures but is present at birth, does not expand and never causes shock. This baby needs urgent transfer for resuscitation.
w: Wrong - caput is scalp oedema present at birth that crosses sutures but does not enlarge or cause shock.
Wrong - a cephalohaematoma is subperiosteal, so it is limited by the suture lines and does not cause haemodynamic compromise.
Correct - an expanding, boggy swelling crossing sutures after vacuum delivery with tachycardia and pallor indicates subgaleal bleeding.
Wrong - a chignon is a localised artificial caput at the cup site; it is not boggy over the whole scalp and does not cause shock.
Wrong - an encephalocele is a midline defect present from birth, not an enlarging swelling with hypovolaemia.

mcq.stem:
A 3-week-old girl, first-born and delivered by caesarean section for breech presentation, attends the Klinik Kesihatan. With the hip adducted and gentle posterior pressure applied, the left femoral head slips out of the acetabulum with a palpable clunk. The thigh skin folds are asymmetrical.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Refer for hip ultrasound and orthopaedic review
Advise double nappies and review at the 6-month visit
Arrange an anteroposterior pelvic X-ray today
Reassure that maternal hormones cause transient hip laxity
Repeat both hip manoeuvres at the 2-month visit
mcq.e: A positive Barlow test (a located but dislocatable hip) in a breech, first-born girl means developmental dysplasia of the hip until proven otherwise. Ultrasound is the imaging of choice under about 4-6 months because the femoral head is still cartilage, and early orthopaedic treatment (e.g., Pavlik harness) gives the best result. Waiting or double nappies risks a missed dislocation.
w: Correct - an unstable hip with risk factors needs hip ultrasound and orthopaedic assessment now.
Wrong - double nappies are not a treatment, and waiting 6 months loses the best window for harness treatment.
Wrong - the infant femoral head is not ossified, so X-ray is unreliable before about 4-6 months.
Wrong - some laxity is common, but a clunk with asymmetric folds in a high-risk girl cannot simply be reassured.
Wrong - an abnormal manoeuvre should not be rechecked later; it needs imaging and specialist review.

mcq.stem:
A 4-day-old boy is reviewed at a home visit. He fed poorly today and is slightly tachypnoeic. The right brachial pulse is easily felt but both femoral pulses are weak and delayed. Pre-ductal SpO2 is 98% and post-ductal SpO2 is 91%.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Ventricular septal defect
Patent ductus arteriosus
Atrial septal defect
Tetralogy of Fallot
Coarctation of the aorta
mcq.e: Weak or delayed femoral pulses compared with the right arm, and lower post-ductal saturation, point to coarctation of the aorta. It often presents on days 2-7 as the ductus arteriosus closes, causing heart failure or shock. This is why femoral pulses are palpated at every newborn check, and the baby needs same-day referral for echocardiography.
w: Wrong - a VSD causes a pansystolic murmur and does not reduce femoral pulses.
Wrong - a PDA gives bounding, not weak, peripheral pulses.
Wrong - an ASD is usually silent in the newborn and does not affect femoral pulses.
Wrong - tetralogy causes central cyanosis with equal pulses, not a pre-/post-ductal difference with weak femorals.
Correct - weak femorals with radio-femoral delay and a post-ductal SpO2 drop suggest coarctation as the duct closes.

mcq.stem:
At a 5-day home visit, a term baby girl looks well and is feeding. On ophthalmoscopy the right eye shows a normal red reflex but the left pupil reflects white. The mother had a fever and rash in the first trimester.
What is the most appropriate action?
o: Repeat the red reflex at the 6-week check
Urgent referral to an ophthalmologist
Chloramphenicol eye ointment and review in 1 week
TORCH serology first, then refer if positive
Routine eye clinic appointment at 3 months
mcq.e: An absent or white red reflex (leukocoria) needs urgent ophthalmology referral: the main causes are congenital cataract (here possibly congenital rubella) and retinoblastoma. Cataract must be removed within the first weeks to prevent dense amblyopia, and retinoblastoma is life-threatening. Investigations for the cause should not delay referral.
w: Wrong - waiting until 6 weeks risks irreversible amblyopia or a delayed cancer diagnosis.
Correct - leukocoria is an emergency referral for cataract or retinoblastoma.
Wrong - antibiotics treat conjunctivitis, not an abnormal red reflex.
Wrong - serology may be useful later, but it must not delay referral.
Wrong - a routine 3-month appointment is too late for congenital cataract surgery.

mcq.stem:
A 3-week-old boy, born by difficult breech delivery, is brought to the Klinik Kesihatan because his head always tilts to the right with the chin turned to the left. There is a firm, non-tender, olive-sized mass within the right sternomastoid muscle. He is feeding well and the rest of the examination is normal.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the neck mass to exclude tumour
Urgent surgical release of the sternomastoid
Cervical spine X-ray and a soft cervical collar
Passive stretching exercises taught to the parents
Oral antibiotics for cervical lymphadenitis
mcq.e: A firm lump in the sternomastoid with head tilt towards and chin away from the lesion is a sternomastoid tumour causing congenital muscular torticollis. Most resolve within a year with parent-taught passive stretching and positioning, supervised by physiotherapy. Surgery is reserved for persistent cases after about a year.
w: Wrong - the clinical picture is typical; biopsy is unnecessary and invasive.
Wrong - surgical release is only for torticollis persisting despite months of stretching.
Wrong - a collar has no role and the lesion is muscular, not bony.
Correct - stretching and positioning resolve most sternomastoid tumours.
Wrong - the mass lies within the muscle, is non-tender and the baby is well, so this is not infection.

mcq.stem:
A 2-day-old boy is examined before discharge. The urethral meatus opens on the ventral surface of the glans and the foreskin is hooded dorsally. Both testes are palpable in the scrotum. The family plans to circumcise him next week.
What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Defer circumcision and refer to paediatric surgery
Proceed with the circumcision as the family planned
Send an urgent karyotype before any further plans
Reassure that the meatus will migrate by puberty
Arrange an urgent renal ultrasound and MCUG
mcq.e: Hypospadias must not be circumcised because the foreskin is used in the surgical repair, usually done at 6-18 months. Isolated distal hypospadias with both testes palpable does not need urgent karyotyping. If testes were impalpable, a disorder of sex development (e.g., CAH) would need urgent assessment.
w: Correct - the foreskin is needed for the repair, so circumcision is postponed and the baby referred.
Wrong - circumcision removes tissue the surgeon needs for reconstruction.
Wrong - karyotyping is needed when hypospadias occurs with impalpable testes, not here.
Wrong - the meatus does not move; untreated hypospadias causes spraying and chordee.
Wrong - isolated distal hypospadias is not an indication for urgent urinary tract imaging.

mcq.stem:
At a newborn check, a 1-day-old girl's right foot is turned inward and downward. Gently, the foot can be passively moved to the neutral position and beyond, and normal skin creases are present. The calf looks normal and both hips are stable.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Refer for Ponseti serial casting this week
Arrange an X-ray of both feet
Refer to orthopaedics for Achilles tenotomy
Reassure and teach gentle stretching exercises
Spinal ultrasound to look for occult spina bifida first
mcq.e: A foot that can be passively corrected to neutral is positional talipes, caused by intrauterine posture, and resolves with simple stretching. CTEV (club foot) is rigid, cannot be corrected, and needs early Ponseti casting with tenotomy. Passive correctability is the key bedside discriminator.
w: Wrong - casting is for rigid CTEV, not a fully correctable positional foot.
Wrong - X-rays add nothing in a correctable newborn foot.
Wrong - tenotomy is part of Ponseti treatment for true CTEV.
Correct - a passively correctable foot is positional talipes, managed with reassurance and stretching.
Wrong - an isolated correctable foot with a normal spine does not suggest dysraphism.

mcq.stem:
A 2-day-old baby boy, 4.3 kg, was born after shoulder dystocia. His right arm lies limp at his side, internally rotated with the wrist flexed. The Moro reflex is absent on the right but present on the left, and the right palmar grasp is present. There is no clavicular tenderness or crepitus.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Klumpke palsy (C8-T1)
Erb palsy (C5-C6)
Fractured right clavicle
Septic arthritis of the shoulder
Right hemiplegic cerebral palsy
mcq.e: An asymmetric Moro reflex after shoulder dystocia with a 'waiter's tip' posture and a preserved grasp is Erb palsy from upper brachial plexus (C5-C6) injury. Klumpke palsy affects C8-T1, so the grasp is lost. A fractured clavicle also gives an asymmetric Moro but with local tenderness or crepitus.
w: Wrong - lower plexus injury causes a claw hand with an absent grasp.
Correct - a waiter's tip posture with an intact grasp localises the lesion to C5-C6.
Wrong - a clavicle fracture gives tenderness or crepitus, which are absent here.
Wrong - septic arthritis causes pseudoparalysis with fever and a swollen, painful joint, not on day 2 after dystocia.
Wrong - hemiplegia is not diagnosed on day 2 and does not give this posture after a traumatic delivery.

mcq.stem:
A 3-week-old term boy attends the Klinik Kesihatan because his umbilicus is always wet. The cord separated on day 9. Clear, odourless fluid leaks from the umbilicus, more so when he cries. There is no surrounding redness and no granulation tissue is seen.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Umbilical granuloma
Omphalitis
Umbilical hernia
Patent vitello-intestinal duct
Patent urachus
mcq.e: A patent urachus is a persistent connection between the bladder and umbilicus, so clear urine leaks, especially when abdominal pressure rises with crying. It needs referral to paediatric surgery. A granuloma is a moist pink nodule treated with silver nitrate, and a vitello-intestinal duct leaks mucus or faecal material.
w: Wrong - a granuloma is a visible pink fleshy nodule, which is absent here.
Wrong - omphalitis causes spreading periumbilical redness and discharge with possible sepsis.
Wrong - an umbilical hernia is a reducible swelling and does not leak fluid.
Wrong - a vitello-intestinal duct connects to the ileum and discharges mucus or stool, not clear fluid.
Correct - clear fluid that increases with crying is urine from a patent urachus.

mcq.stem:
A term baby boy, discharged early after delivery, is seen by the community nurse at home at 18 hours of life. The mother is group O Rh-positive and this is her first pregnancy. The baby's face and chest look yellow. He is feeding and active.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Reassure and review on the planned day-3 home visit
Advise frequent feeds and morning sunlight exposure
Same-day referral for serum bilirubin and workup
Repeat the Kramer assessment in 24 hours
Check the cord G6PD result and review in 2 days
mcq.e: Jaundice appearing within 24 hours of life is always pathological and needs urgent attention, because physiological jaundice never appears this early. The likely cause here is haemolysis from ABO incompatibility, which can occur in a first pregnancy. Serum bilirubin, blood groups, direct Coombs test, FBC and reticulocytes are needed the same day.
w: Wrong - physiological jaundice never starts before 24 hours, so reassurance is unsafe.
Wrong - sunlight is not a treatment, and feeding advice alone ignores likely haemolysis.
Correct - early-onset jaundice is pathological and needs urgent serum bilirubin and haemolysis tests.
Wrong - early jaundice can rise rapidly, so waiting 24 hours risks kernicterus.
Wrong - G6PD is one cause, but a normal result would not make early jaundice safe to watch.

mcq.stem:
A 1-day-old term girl has jaundice noted at 20 hours. Her mother is group O Rh-positive and it is her first pregnancy; the baby is group B Rh-positive. Investigations: direct Coombs test weakly positive, reticulocytes raised, spherocytes on the blood film. Cord G6PD screening was normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Rhesus isoimmunisation
G6PD deficiency
Hereditary spherocytosis
Breast milk jaundice
ABO incompatibility
mcq.e: An O mother with an A or B baby, a positive direct Coombs test and spherocytes indicates ABO haemolytic disease. Maternal anti-A/anti-B IgG is naturally present, so it can affect the first pregnancy, unlike Rh disease which needs prior sensitisation. Spherocytes occur in ABO disease too, so a positive Coombs test makes hereditary spherocytosis less likely.
w: Wrong - both mother and baby are Rh-positive and Rh disease usually spares the first pregnancy.
Wrong - cord G6PD screening was normal and G6PD haemolysis is Coombs-negative.
Wrong - hereditary spherocytosis is Coombs-negative; spherocytes also appear in ABO disease.
Wrong - breast milk jaundice starts late in the first week, not at 20 hours.
Correct - O mother, B baby, positive Coombs test and spherocytes indicate ABO incompatibility.

mcq.stem:
A 4-day-old term boy is seen at a home visit. He is breastfeeding 10 times a day, is active and has yellow stools. Jaundice extends to the lower abdomen. The nurse's transcutaneous bilirubin (TcB) reading is 230 µmol/L.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Repeat the TcB at the day-8 home visit
Stop breastfeeding for 48 hours
Measure total serum bilirubin
Start phototherapy based on the TcB alone
Reassure as the baby is well and feeding
mcq.e: TcB is the screening tool whenever jaundice is seen, but if TcB exceeds 200 µmol/L (12 mg/dL) a total serum bilirubin must be measured and plotted on the hour-specific treatment chart. TcB is less accurate at higher levels, so treatment decisions rest on the serum value. A well baby can still have a level needing phototherapy.
w: Wrong - a TcB above 200 µmol/L requires a serum level now, not in 4 days.
Wrong - stopping breastfeeding is not the response to a high screening value and risks lactation failure.
Correct - TcB above 200 µmol/L must be confirmed with a total serum bilirubin.
Wrong - phototherapy decisions use the serum bilirubin plotted on the chart, not TcB.
Wrong - looking well does not exclude a bilirubin level near the treatment threshold.

mcq.stem:
A 6-day-old term girl was discharged yesterday after 2 days of hospital phototherapy for haemolytic jaundice. At the Klinik Kesihatan the nurse suggests a transcutaneous bilirubin (TcB) reading to check for rebound.
Why is TcB unreliable in this baby?
o: Skin bilirubin is bleached, so TcB underestimates serum levels
Skin bilirubin rises under the lights, so TcB overestimates serum levels
TcB measures only the conjugated fraction of bilirubin
TcB cannot be used in babies with haemolytic disease
TcB readings are invalid in babies older than 5 days
mcq.e: Phototherapy acts first on bilirubin in the skin, so TcB falls faster than serum bilirubin and gives false reassurance. The slides state that TcB should not be used to monitor babies on phototherapy; serum bilirubin is used during and soon after treatment. Haemolysing babies are at particular risk of rebound.
w: Correct - skin bleaching makes TcB read falsely low after phototherapy.
Wrong - phototherapy lowers skin bilirubin; the error is underestimation.
Wrong - TcB estimates total bilirubin from skin colour, not the conjugated fraction.
Wrong - haemolysis does not invalidate TcB; prior phototherapy does.
Wrong - TcB is used well beyond day 5; age is not the problem here.

mcq.stem:
A 4-week-old term boy attends the Klinik Kesihatan with jaundice since the second week. He is breastfed and gaining weight. The mother shows his stool, which matches the palest shade on the stool colour card, and his urine stains the nappy dark yellow. The liver is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Diagnose breast milk jaundice and stop breastfeeding for 48 hours
Repeat a transcutaneous bilirubin in 2 weeks
Start home phototherapy and review in 1 week
Same-week referral for split bilirubin and liver assessment
Give oral vitamin K and recheck at the 2-month visit
mcq.e: Prolonged jaundice with pale (acholic) stools, dark urine and hepatomegaly suggests conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia from biliary atresia. Kasai portoenterostomy works best before about 60 days of age, so referral must be urgent. Phototherapy is useless for conjugated jaundice, and a thriving baby does not exclude biliary atresia.
w: Wrong - breast milk jaundice gives yellow stools and normal urine, not acholic stools.
Wrong - a 2-week delay may push surgery beyond the 60-day window.
Wrong - phototherapy does not treat conjugated bilirubin.
Correct - pale stools and dark urine need urgent conjugated bilirubin and biliary assessment.
Wrong - vitamin K may be needed, but it does not address the likely biliary obstruction.

mcq.stem:
A 3-week-old exclusively breastfed term girl is still yellow to the chest. She is feeding well, has gained 600 g since birth, and passes yellow stools and pale urine. Investigations: total bilirubin 190 µmol/L, conjugated 12 µmol/L, cord TSH and G6PD normal, urinalysis normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Biliary atresia
Breast milk jaundice
Congenital hypothyroidism
Neonatal hepatitis
Suboptimal breastfeeding jaundice
mcq.e: A thriving breastfed baby with prolonged unconjugated jaundice, normal stools and urine, and normal thyroid and G6PD results most likely has breast milk jaundice. It begins late in the first week, peaks at 2-3 weeks and is due to increased enterohepatic circulation. Breastfeeding should continue; the prolonged-jaundice screen is still done, as here.
w: Wrong - biliary atresia causes conjugated bilirubin above 34 µmol/L with pale stools.
Correct - well, gaining weight, unconjugated and with a normal screen fits breast milk jaundice.
Wrong - cord TSH was normal and hypothyroidism causes poor feeding and constipation.
Wrong - neonatal hepatitis gives conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.
Wrong - poor-intake jaundice occurs in the first week with weight loss, not good weight gain.

mcq.stem:
A 5-day-old Malay boy with G6PD deficiency on cord blood screening is seen at a home visit. His bilirubin was checked yesterday and was below the phototherapy line. His grandmother is preparing the baby's clothes cupboard and a traditional bath for him.
Which advice is most important to prevent severe jaundice?
o: Give plain water between breastfeeds
Avoid naphthalene mothballs and herbal remedies
Place the baby in morning sunlight each day
Withhold all routine vaccines until 6 months of age
Change to formula feeding until 6 weeks
mcq.e: G6PD deficiency causes sudden, severe haemolysis when the baby meets oxidant triggers, and is a major cause of kernicterus in Malaysia. Naphthalene (mothballs on clothes) and some traditional herbal remedies are classic triggers. Breastfeeding and vaccination continue normally, and sunlight does not treat jaundice.
w: Wrong - plain water displaces milk and can worsen jaundice.
Correct - avoiding oxidant triggers such as mothballs and herbs prevents acute haemolysis.
Wrong - sunlight is not an effective or safe treatment and delays care.
Wrong - G6PD deficiency is not a contraindication to any routine vaccine.
Wrong - breastfeeding is safe, although a mother should avoid trigger foods and drugs.

mcq.stem:
A 5-day-old term boy is brought to the Klinik Kesihatan with deep jaundice to the soles. He is drowsy, feeds poorly, has a high-pitched cry and arches his neck and back backwards when handled. Temperature 37.0 °C. Serum bilirubin is 430 µmol/L.
What is the most appropriate action?
o: Start phototherapy in the clinic and repeat serum bilirubin in 6 hours
Increase breastfeeding and arrange a home visit in 24 hours
Admit for oral phenobarbitone to induce liver enzymes
Give a bolus of 10% dextrose and recheck bilirubin tomorrow
Emergency transfer for intensive phototherapy and exchange transfusion
mcq.e: Drowsiness, poor feeding, a high-pitched cry and opisthotonus are signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy (intermediate phase, a moderate-severe BIND score). Unbound unconjugated bilirubin has crossed the blood-brain barrier, so the baby needs emergency transfer for intensive phototherapy and urgent exchange transfusion to prevent kernicterus. Every hour of delay matters.
w: Wrong - clinics cannot give intensive phototherapy, and waiting 6 hours risks permanent damage.
Wrong - feeding advice alone is dangerous when signs of encephalopathy are present.
Wrong - phenobarbitone acts too slowly and has no role in acute encephalopathy.
Wrong - dextrose does not lower bilirubin, and a next-day recheck is far too late.
Correct - neurological signs with severe jaundice require intensive phototherapy and exchange transfusion now.

mcq.stem:
A term baby boy had a serum bilirubin of 120 µmol/L at 36 hours and 260 µmol/L at 60 hours of life. Cord blood G6PD screening was normal. He is well and feeding. You are arranging further tests to find the cause.
Which investigation is most useful next?
o: Conjugated (direct) bilirubin level
Thyroid function test
Ultrasound of the liver and biliary tree to look for obstruction
Blood groups of mother and baby with a direct Coombs test
TORCH serology
mcq.e: A rise of 140 µmol/L in 24 hours exceeds the 103 µmol/L per 24 h threshold, so this is pathological jaundice with a rapid rise, which suggests haemolysis. The slides recommend G6PD (already normal here), mother's and baby's blood groups, a direct Coombs test, FBC with film and reticulocytes. Biliary and thyroid tests belong to prolonged jaundice.
w: Wrong - a conjugated level matters in prolonged jaundice; a rapid early rise is usually unconjugated haemolysis.
Wrong - hypothyroidism causes prolonged jaundice, not a rapid rise on day 2-3.
Wrong - biliary imaging is for conjugated or prolonged jaundice with pale stools.
Correct - a rapid rise suggests isoimmune haemolysis, shown by blood groups and the Coombs test.
Wrong - TORCH causes conjugated jaundice with other signs such as petechiae and hepatosplenomegaly.

mcq.stem:
A baby girl born at 34 weeks' gestation is reviewed at the Klinik Kesihatan on day 18. She is well, breastfeeding and gaining weight, with yellow stools and pale urine. Mild yellowing is seen on the face only; TcB is 110 µmol/L.
What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Start the prolonged jaundice workup today
Refer for phototherapy
Continue feeds; review if jaundice persists beyond day 21
Stop breastfeeding for 48 hours to confirm breast milk jaundice
Urgent abdominal ultrasound for biliary atresia
mcq.e: Prolonged jaundice is visible jaundice persisting beyond 14 days in a term baby but beyond 21 days in a preterm baby, because preterm physiological jaundice lasts up to 3 weeks. This well preterm baby with normal stools and urine on day 18 does not yet meet the definition. Pale stools or dark urine at any age would change this and need urgent review.
w: Wrong - for a preterm baby the prolonged jaundice cut-off is 21 days, not 14.
Wrong - a TcB of 110 µmol/L on day 18 is far below phototherapy thresholds.
Correct - a well preterm baby with normal stools is reviewed if jaundice continues beyond day 21.
Wrong - interrupting breastfeeding is not needed and may harm lactation.
Wrong - normal stool and urine colour make biliary atresia unlikely.

mcq.stem:
A first-time mother at a day-4 home visit is worried because her well, breastfed term son turned yellow yesterday. He has fed well, passed yellow stools and the jaundice is limited to the face and chest. She asks why healthy babies become jaundiced.
Which explanation is correct?
o: Rapid red cell breakdown with an immature liver
A temporary blockage of the bile ducts in the first week
Antibodies in breast milk that break down red cells
Bilirubin from the mother's blood crossing in breast milk
Not enough sunlight in the first days after birth
mcq.e: Physiological jaundice comes from increased bilirubin production (higher haemoglobin and a shorter red cell lifespan) with immature hepatic conjugation and clearance. It appears 2-4 days after birth and resolves in 1-2 weeks in term babies (up to 3 weeks preterm). The baby stays well, feeds well and has normal stools.
w: Correct - high red cell turnover with an immature liver explains physiological jaundice.
Wrong - bile duct obstruction causes conjugated jaundice with pale stools and is never physiological.
Wrong - breast milk does not contain antibodies that destroy the baby's red cells.
Wrong - maternal bilirubin is not passed in breast milk to cause jaundice.
Wrong - lack of sunlight does not cause jaundice and sunlight is not a treatment.

mcq.stem:
A child is brought to the Klinik Kesihatan for a routine developmental check. He walks without help but cannot yet run steadily. He builds a tower of 3 cubes, uses about 15 single words, feeds himself with a spoon and 'feeds' his doll. He does not yet join two words together.
Which age do these milestones best match?
o: 12 months
18 months
2 years
3 years
9 months
mcq.e: Walking unassisted, a 2-3 cube tower, 10-20 words, spoon feeding and simple pretend play are the 18-month milestones on the slides. At 2 years a child runs, builds 6 cubes and joins 2 words; at 12 months a child cruises or stands and says 1-3 words. Matching across all four domains, rather than one skill, gives the developmental age.
w: Wrong - at 12 months a child cruises or stands alone and says only 1-3 words.
Correct - independent walking, 2-3 cubes, 10-20 words and pretend play fit 18 months.
Wrong - a 2-year-old runs, builds 6 cubes and joins 2 words.
Wrong - a 3-year-old rides a tricycle and speaks in 3-4 word sentences.
Wrong - a 9-month-old sits, uses an inferior pincer and does not yet walk or speak words.

mcq.stem:
A 10-month-old girl attends her routine KKIA check. She rolls both ways and holds her head well. Placed on the floor, she topples over unless propped with cushions. She babbles 'ba-ba', transfers toys between hands and plays peek-a-boo.
Which finding is the developmental red flag?
o: She has no meaningful single words yet
She is not yet walking or cruising
She does not use a neat pincer grasp
She cannot sit without support
She is not yet drinking from an open cup
mcq.e: Inability to sit without support by 9-12 months is a gross motor red flag on the slides; most babies sit unsupported by 6-8 months. Words, cruising, a neat pincer grasp and cup drinking are expected around 12 months, so their absence at 10 months is normal. The child needs a full neurological examination and referral.
w: Wrong - first meaningful words are expected around 12 months, not 10.
Wrong - cruising and walking come at about 12 months; not walking is a red flag only at 18 months.
Wrong - a neat pincer grasp is a 12-month skill; an inferior pincer at 9-10 months is normal.
Correct - not sitting unsupported by 9-12 months is a red flag needing assessment.
Wrong - drinking from a cup is a 12-month milestone.

mcq.stem:
A 10-month-old boy, born at term after a difficult labour, attends the Klinik Kesihatan. His mother is pleased that he is already 'right-handed': he reaches for every toy with his right hand. His left hand is often fisted and he rarely uses it, even for large toys placed on his left.
What is the most likely explanation?
o: Left-sided hemiplegic cerebral palsy
Early right-hand dominance, a normal variant
Right brachial plexus (Erb) palsy
Developmental coordination disorder
Autism spectrum disorder
mcq.e: Hand preference before about 12-18 months is a red flag, because infants normally use both hands until handedness emerges later. A clear preference usually means the other hand is weak. A fisted, neglected left hand points to a left hemiplegia, often hemiplegic cerebral palsy from a right brain lesion, and needs neurological examination and referral.
w: Correct - an early preference with a fisted, unused left hand suggests left hemiplegia.
Wrong - true hand dominance does not appear this early; early preference implies weakness.
Wrong - the weak side is the left, and Erb palsy would have been noted from birth with an arm posture, not a fisted hand.
Wrong - DCD is diagnosed in older children with clumsiness, not unilateral weakness in infancy.
Wrong - ASD affects social communication and does not cause one-sided hand neglect.

mcq.stem:
A 26-month-old girl is brought to the Klinik Kesihatan. Her mother says she spoke about 20 words at 18 months but now says none. Over the last 4 months she has stopped using her hands to feed herself and makes repetitive hand-wringing movements. Her head circumference has dropped from the 50th to the 9th centile.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Reassure and review her speech in 3 months
Refer for speech therapy and review in 6 months
Arrange a hearing test and review the result first
Advise less screen time and more talking at home
Urgent referral to a paediatrician for assessment
mcq.e: Loss of previously acquired skills (regression) at any age is a red flag needing urgent specialist referral. Regression of speech and hand use with stereotyped hand-wringing and slowing head growth in a girl suggests Rett syndrome, but neurodegenerative and metabolic disorders and ASD must also be considered. Speech therapy or a hearing test alone would miss the diagnosis.
w: Wrong - regression is never managed by watchful waiting.
Wrong - therapy may help later, but regression needs urgent diagnostic assessment first.
Wrong - hearing loss does not cause loss of hand skills or falling head growth.
Wrong - environmental advice does not explain regression of speech and hand use.
Correct - loss of skills plus decelerating head growth requires urgent paediatric referral.

mcq.stem:
A 2-year-old boy is reviewed at the Klinik Kesihatan because he says only 'mama' and 'papa'. He walks, runs and climbs well, makes good eye contact, points to show his mother things and brings her toys to play. He passed newborn hearing screening. His grandmother says his father also talked late.
What is the most appropriate first investigation?
o: MRI of the brain
Electroencephalogram
Formal audiological assessment
Karyotype and fragile X testing
Thyroid function tests
mcq.e: In a child with isolated speech delay the first investigation is a formal hearing assessment, even if the newborn screen was passed, because hearing loss can be acquired (e.g., glue ear) and is treatable. Normal social communication makes ASD less likely. Imaging, EEG and genetic tests are guided by other findings such as regression, seizures or dysmorphism.
w: Wrong - neuroimaging is not a first-line test for isolated speech delay with normal examination.
Wrong - EEG is indicated for seizures or regression, not isolated speech delay.
Correct - hearing must be tested first in any child with speech delay.
Wrong - genetic tests are for global delay or dysmorphism, not isolated speech delay.
Wrong - hypothyroidism causes global slowing and poor growth, not isolated speech delay.

mcq.stem:
A baby girl born at 28 weeks' gestation is now 6 months old (chronological age) and attends the KKIA. She has good head control, smiles responsively, follows objects and is starting to roll over. She cannot yet sit, even with support, and does not yet transfer objects between her hands.
What is the best interpretation of her development?
o: Delayed: judge against 6-month milestones
Delayed: refer for global developmental delay
Delayed: start physiotherapy for poor sitting
Appropriate: judge against 3-month milestones
Appropriate only if she sits by 7 months
mcq.e: Development in a preterm baby is assessed by corrected age (chronological age minus weeks born early) until about 2 years. Born 12 weeks early, this 6-month-old has a corrected age of about 3 months, and her skills fit that age. Immunisations, in contrast, follow chronological age.
w: Wrong - using chronological age labels preterm babies falsely delayed.
Wrong - she meets her corrected-age milestones, so there is no global delay.
Wrong - sitting is not expected at a corrected age of 3 months.
Correct - at a corrected age of about 3 months her development is appropriate.
Wrong - sitting by 7 months chronological age is not expected in a baby born 12 weeks early.

mcq.stem:
A 2-week-old baby boy is seen at the Klinik Kesihatan. He was born in a district hospital and discharged at 12 hours of life. The Child Health Record Book shows that the newborn hearing screen was not done. He startles to loud noises at home.
What is the most appropriate action?
o: Arrange AABR/OAE screening within the first month
Rely on his startle and test only if speech is delayed
Defer testing to the distraction test at 7-9 months
Test at 18 months together with the M-CHAT screen
Refer for MRI of the inner ear and auditory nerve
mcq.e: Universal Newborn Hearing Screening with automated AABR or OAE is done before discharge or within the first month of life. Startling to noise does not exclude significant hearing loss. Early screening allows diagnosis by 3 months and intervention by 6 months, protecting language development.
w: Correct - a missed screen should be completed with AABR/OAE within the first month.
Wrong - a startle response can occur with partial hearing loss, and waiting for speech delay is too late.
Wrong - the distraction test is outdated and far too late for early intervention.
Wrong - 18 months misses the critical early window for language.
Wrong - imaging is not a screening test and is only used after confirmed hearing loss.

mcq.stem:
At a routine KKIA visit you check the milestones of a healthy 3-year-old girl born at term. Her mother asks what she should be able to do now.
Which skill is expected at this age?
o: Copies a cross and a square
Hops several times on one foot
Rides a tricycle
Skips with alternating feet
Writes her own name
mcq.e: At 3 years the slides list standing briefly on one foot, riding a tricycle, copying a circle, 3-4 word sentences, asking 'why' and dressing with minimal help. Hopping and copying a cross come at about 4 years; a square, skipping and name writing at about 4-5 years. Knowing the next milestone helps avoid over-referral.
w: Wrong - copying a cross is a 4-year skill and a square comes later.
Wrong - hopping repeatedly is a 4-year skill; at 3 she stands briefly on one foot.
Correct - riding a tricycle is a 3-year milestone.
Wrong - skipping is expected at about 5 years.
Wrong - writing her name is a 5-year skill.

mcq.stem:
A 30-month-old boy is assessed at the Klinik Kesihatan. He walked at 24 months, says about 10 single words, cannot use a spoon and does not yet play pretend games. Hearing and vision are normal and he has no dysmorphic features.
Which term best describes his development?
o: Intellectual disability
Global developmental delay
Specific language impairment
Developmental coordination disorder
Isolated gross motor delay
mcq.e: Significant delay in two or more domains (here gross motor, speech and social/self-help) in a child under 5 years is called global developmental delay. Intellectual disability is a diagnosis made in older children with formal cognitive testing. The child needs paediatric referral, investigation and early intervention.
w: Wrong - intellectual disability is diagnosed by formal testing, usually after 5 years.
Correct - delay in two or more domains under age 5 is global developmental delay.
Wrong - his delays extend beyond language to motor and self-help skills.
Wrong - DCD is a motor coordination disorder of school-age children with otherwise normal development.
Wrong - his delays involve several domains, not just gross motor.

mcq.stem:
An 18-month-old boy is brought to the Klinik Kesihatan because he cannot walk alone. He sat at 9 months and crawls well. He has 12 words and good social interaction. On examination he has bulky calves and mild proximal weakness, and he pushes on his thighs to stand up from the floor.
Which investigation is most useful first?
o: Serum calcium and vitamin D
X-ray of both hips
Thyroid function test
MRI of the brain
Serum creatine kinase
mcq.e: Not walking by 18 months is a red flag. In a boy with calf pseudohypertrophy, proximal weakness and a Gowers' sign, Duchenne muscular dystrophy is likely, and a markedly raised creatine kinase is the simple first test. Early diagnosis allows genetic counselling and specialist care.
w: Wrong - rickets can delay walking but does not cause calf hypertrophy and a Gowers' sign.
Wrong - DDH causes a limp or leg asymmetry, not proximal weakness.
Wrong - hypothyroidism causes global slowing and poor growth, not this pattern.
Wrong - his normal speech and social skills do not suggest a brain lesion.
Correct - creatine kinase is the first test for suspected Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

mcq.stem:
A 3-month-old girl attends the Klinik Kesihatan for her scheduled vaccines. She has had a runny nose and an occasional cough for 3 days. She is feeding well and active. Temperature 37.2 °C, RR 38/min, chest clear.
What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give the due vaccines today as scheduled
Defer all vaccines until the cough settles
Give only the oral or inactivated components today
Give prophylactic antibiotics, then vaccinate
Defer vaccines for 1 week and give paracetamol
mcq.e: Mild illness without fever, such as a cold, cough or mild diarrhoea, is a false contraindication. Deferring vaccines for minor illness is a common missed opportunity that leaves infants unprotected. Only an acute febrile, moderate-to-severe illness justifies postponement.
w: Correct - an afebrile mild illness is not a reason to delay vaccination.
Wrong - deferral for a mild cold is a missed opportunity.
Wrong - all the due vaccines can be given; the illness is not a contraindication.
Wrong - antibiotics are not indicated and are not needed before vaccines.
Wrong - there is no reason to delay, and routine paracetamol is not required.

mcq.stem:
A 5-month-old boy is brought for his scheduled vaccines. Since yesterday he has had a fever of 39.2 °C, is irritable, feeding less and has vomited twice. HR 170/min. There is no rash.
What is the most appropriate action regarding his vaccines?
o: Give all due vaccines today with paracetamol
Give only the inactivated vaccines today
Give the vaccines and review him tomorrow
Give half doses today and the rest next week
Postpone until he has recovered from the illness
mcq.e: An acute febrile illness is a reason to postpone vaccination until recovery. This avoids confusing vaccine reactions with the illness and allows the febrile infant to be properly assessed, here for possible sepsis. It is a temporary deferral, not a contraindication.
w: Wrong - acute febrile illness is a reason to postpone, and paracetamol does not change that.
Wrong - the postponement rule applies to all vaccines in acute febrile illness.
Wrong - this unwell febrile infant needs assessment, not vaccination.
Wrong - split or half doses are never used.
Correct - vaccines are postponed in acute febrile illness and given after recovery.

mcq.stem:
A 12-month-old girl is due her second MMR dose at the Klinik Kesihatan. Her grandfather was recently diagnosed with smear-positive pulmonary TB, and a Mantoux test was placed on her forearm yesterday as part of contact screening.
What is the most appropriate plan for her MMR?
o: Give MMR today as scheduled
Give MMR today and repeat the Mantoux in 4 weeks
Omit MMR until TB is excluded with a chest X-ray
Delay MMR until the Mantoux has been read
Postpone MMR for 3 months after the Mantoux
mcq.e: Measles vaccine temporarily suppresses cell-mediated immunity and can cause a false-negative Mantoux test. If a Mantoux has already been placed, MMR is delayed until it has been read (48-72 hours). If MMR is given first, wait at least 4 weeks before doing a Mantoux.
w: Wrong - giving MMR now could suppress the Mantoux reaction and mask TB infection.
Wrong - the existing test should be read first rather than repeated later.
Wrong - MMR is only delayed until the test is read, not until a full TB workup is complete.
Correct - MMR waits until the Mantoux is read, which takes 48-72 hours.
Wrong - a 3-month delay is unnecessary and leaves her unprotected.

mcq.stem:
Five children are due their MMR vaccine at a Klinik Kesihatan clinic session.
Which child should NOT receive MMR today?
o: A 9-month-old with egg allergy who had hives after eating egg
A 12-month-old on inhaled budesonide for wheeze
A 4-year-old with ALL on maintenance chemotherapy
A 12-month-old whose mother is 20 weeks pregnant
A 9-month-old with one previous febrile convulsion
mcq.e: Live vaccines such as MMR are contraindicated in immunosuppressed children, including those with leukaemia on chemotherapy, after transplant or with primary immunodeficiency. Egg allergy, inhaled steroids, a pregnant mother and a history of febrile convulsions are all false contraindications. Siblings of immunosuppressed children should be vaccinated to protect them.
w: Wrong - egg allergy is not a contraindication to MMR, which contains negligible egg protein.
Wrong - inhaled or topical steroids do not cause significant immunosuppression.
Correct - leukaemia on chemotherapy is a contraindication to live vaccines.
Wrong - a child's mother being pregnant is not a reason to withhold the child's vaccines.
Wrong - febrile convulsions and stable neurological conditions are not contraindications.

mcq.stem:
A 3-month-old boy is due his second dose of DTaP-IPV-Hib-HepB. After the first dose his mother noticed a 2 cm red, slightly tender area on the thigh and a temperature of 38.0 °C that settled the next day with paracetamol.
What is the most appropriate action?
o: Withhold all further pertussis-containing doses
Give the next dose as scheduled
Switch to DT vaccine for the remaining doses
Give the next dose in two half-dose injections
Refer to a paediatrician for skin-prick testing first
mcq.e: Killed vaccines are generally safe; a further dose is contraindicated only after anaphylaxis, a severe local reaction involving more than two-thirds of the limb, or a severe generalised reaction. Small local redness and low-grade fever are expected minor reactions. The mother can be reassured and advised on paracetamol for fever.
w: Wrong - minor local reaction and brief fever do not contraindicate pertussis vaccine.
Correct - a mild local reaction and low fever are not contraindications.
Wrong - switching to DT leaves the baby unprotected against pertussis without reason.
Wrong - split doses are not used and do not reduce reactions.
Wrong - skin testing is unnecessary after a minor expected reaction.

mcq.stem:
A baby boy born at 30 weeks' gestation is now 2 months old (chronological age), well and gaining weight after discharge from the neonatal unit. His mother asks whether his vaccines should be delayed until his corrected age is 2 months because he is 'still small'.
What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Delay until his corrected age is 2 months
Delay until he weighs at least 2.5 kg
Give full doses now by chronological age
Give reduced doses now because he is small
Give only BCG and hepatitis B until term-corrected
mcq.e: Preterm babies are immunised according to the schedule by chronological age, irrespective of gestational age, with full doses. Prematurity and low weight are false contraindications, and preterm babies are at higher risk of severe pertussis and other infections, so delay is harmful. Corrected age is used only for developmental assessment.
w: Wrong - corrected age is for development, not immunisation.
Wrong - weight is not a criterion for routine vaccination.
Correct - preterm babies are vaccinated by chronological age with full doses.
Wrong - doses are never reduced for prematurity or size.
Wrong - all vaccines due for chronological age should be given.

mcq.stem:
A 4-year-old girl from a refugee family registers at the Klinik Kesihatan. Her mother says she 'had all her injections' in their home country but has no record, and there is no BCG scar.
How should her immunisation status be managed?
o: Accept the history and give only school-age boosters
Treat her as unimmunised and start a catch-up schedule
Check antibody titres for every vaccine before deciding
Give only MMR, since measles is the main risk
Wait for records from the home country before vaccinating
mcq.e: Children whose immunisation status is unknown or undocumented are treated as never having been immunised. An age-appropriate catch-up schedule is started, giving priority to measles-containing vaccine. Extra doses in a child who was in fact vaccinated are not harmful.
w: Wrong - an undocumented history cannot be accepted as immunisation.
Correct - undocumented status is treated as unimmunised with catch-up vaccination.
Wrong - routine serology is not required and delays protection.
Wrong - MMR is prioritised, but the full catch-up schedule is still needed.
Wrong - waiting for records leaves her unprotected.

mcq.stem:
During a measles outbreak in a settlement, a 2-year-old boy who has never been vaccinated is brought to the Klinik Kesihatan. His father refuses more than one injection today but agrees to return for the rest.
Which vaccine should be given today?
o: Hepatitis B
DTaP-IPV//Hib
BCG
Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine
MMR
mcq.e: In catch-up immunisation, priority goes to vaccines against highly transmissible diseases such as measles (MMR/MR), before diphtheria-containing vaccines. During an outbreak this is even more urgent. Ideally all due vaccines are given at the same visit at separate sites, but if only one is accepted it should be MMR.
w: Wrong - hepatitis B is important but measles is the priority in an outbreak.
Wrong - diphtheria-containing vaccines come after measles in catch-up priority.
Wrong - BCG is not the priority for a 2-year-old during a measles outbreak.
Wrong - pneumococcal vaccine is less urgent than measles protection here.
Correct - measles-containing vaccine has catch-up priority, especially during an outbreak.

mcq.stem:
A 7-month-old girl on a catch-up schedule received her first dose of DTaP-IPV-Hib-HepB at another clinic 2 weeks ago. Her mother brings her today wanting to 'finish quickly' before moving interstate next month.
When is the earliest the second dose can be given?
o: In 2 weeks, 4 weeks after the first dose
Today, as catch-up allows any interval
Restart the series from dose 1 in 4 weeks
In 2 months, as in the routine schedule
At the new clinic after she turns 1 year
mcq.e: Catch-up vaccines can be given at shorter intervals than the routine schedule, but the minimum interval between two doses of the same vaccine is 4 weeks. Doses given too close together may not count. An interrupted series is continued, never restarted.
w: Correct - the minimum interval between doses of the same vaccine is 4 weeks.
Wrong - a 2-week interval is shorter than the 4-week minimum.
Wrong - an interrupted or delayed series is never restarted.
Wrong - catch-up allows intervals shorter than the routine schedule.
Wrong - delaying until 1 year leaves her unprotected unnecessarily.

mcq.stem:
A 12-month-old boy is due his MMR vaccine. His 5-year-old sister is having chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and lives in the same house. The mother worries the vaccine could infect her daughter.
What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Defer his MMR until his sister finishes chemotherapy
Give monovalent measles vaccine only
Give him immunoglobulin instead of MMR
Give MMR as scheduled to protect his sister
Give MMR and separate the siblings for 6 weeks
mcq.e: Healthy household contacts of immunosuppressed children should be fully vaccinated, including with MMR, to protect the vulnerable child (cocooning). MMR vaccine virus is not transmitted from vaccinated people. Leaving the brother unvaccinated increases the risk that he brings wild measles home.
w: Wrong - deferring leaves both children at risk of wild measles.
Wrong - monovalent measles vaccine offers no safety advantage and less protection.
Wrong - immunoglobulin gives only short-lived protection and is not a substitute.
Correct - vaccinating siblings protects the immunosuppressed child, and MMR virus is not transmitted.
Wrong - separation is unnecessary because MMR vaccine virus does not spread.

mcq.stem:
A 10-month-old boy attends the Klinik Kesihatan for a routine visit. Over 4 months his weight has fallen from the 50th to below the 3rd centile, his length from the 25th to the 15th centile, and his head circumference has stayed on the 50th centile. He is active and interactive, with no dysmorphic features and a normal systemic examination. His mother returned to full-time work 5 months ago and his grandmother now prepares his formula, using fewer scoops than recommended to make the tin last longer.
Which category of cause best explains his growth faltering?
o: Endocrine cause such as congenital hypothyroidism or growth hormone deficiency
Chronic systemic disease such as an unrepaired congenital heart lesion
Non-organic cause from inadequate caloric intake through feeding practice
Genetic syndrome such as Noonan syndrome with primary short stature
Malabsorption from coeliac disease or cow’s milk protein allergy
mcq.e: When weight falls first, length follows more slowly and head circumference is spared, the pattern points to inadequate energy intake. Here a change of caregiver and over-diluted formula give a clear non-organic cause, and examination finds no organic red flags. Endocrine and genetic causes affect length first, with weight relatively preserved.
w: Wrong - endocrine causes slow linear growth first, so weight-for-length is usually preserved or high.
Wrong - a significant heart lesion would give a murmur, tachypnoea or sweating with feeds; examination is normal.
Correct - weight drops before length, head growth is spared, and diluted formula after a caregiver change explains the energy deficit.
Wrong - genetic short stature tracks low from early on and usually shows dysmorphic features; this boy grew normally until 6 months.
Wrong - malabsorption gives chronic diarrhoea, steatorrhoea or blood in stools, none of which is described.

mcq.stem:
An 18-month-old girl born at home in a rural Sabah village is brought to the Klinik Kesihatan. She had no newborn screening. Her length has dropped from the 50th to the 2nd centile, while her weight remains on the 25th centile. She is sluggish, constipated and has dry coarse skin, a large tongue and an umbilical hernia. She sat at 10 months and is not yet walking.
Which selective investigation is most indicated?
o: Thyroid function test (free T4 and TSH)
Full blood count with serum ferritin level
Urinalysis with urine culture
Stool microscopy and stool culture
Chest X-ray and echocardiography
mcq.e: Poor linear growth with relatively preserved weight, plus constipation, dry skin, macroglossia, umbilical hernia and delayed milestones, suggests hypothyroidism. The growth faltering guideline lists thyroid function as the test when linear growth is poor or clinical features suggest hypothyroidism. Missed newborn cord TSH screening makes congenital hypothyroidism a real possibility, so this must not wait.
w: Correct - poor linear growth with hypothyroid features is the stated indication for thyroid function testing.
Wrong - iron deficiency causes pallor and poor appetite but not macroglossia, umbilical hernia or stunting with preserved weight.
Wrong - urinalysis targets occult UTI, which would give fevers or urinary symptoms rather than these features.
Wrong - stool tests are for chronic diarrhoea or blood in stools; she is constipated.
Wrong - imaging of the chest and heart is for suspected cardiorespiratory disease, which is not suggested here.

mcq.stem:
An 11-month-old boy is reviewed at the Klinik Kesihatan 3 weeks after an episode of acute gastroenteritis. Since then he has had 6-8 loose, frothy, sour-smelling stools a day with marked perianal excoriation, and his weight has fallen from the 50th to the 15th centile. He is afebrile and well hydrated. Stool pH is 5.0 and stool reducing substances are positive. There is no blood or mucus in the stool.
Which diagnosis is most likely?
o: Toddler’s diarrhoea
Cow’s milk protein allergy
Coeliac disease (gluten enteropathy)
Chronic Giardia infection
Secondary lactose intolerance
mcq.e: Damage to the brush border after gastroenteritis causes temporary lactase deficiency. Undigested lactose is fermented, giving acidic, frothy stools with positive reducing substances and perianal excoriation. Toddler’s diarrhoea does not cause growth faltering, and the clear trigger and stool chemistry favour lactose intolerance over allergy or coeliac disease.
w: Wrong - toddler’s diarrhoea occurs in thriving children and does not cause growth faltering or acidic stools.
Wrong - cow’s milk protein allergy is usually present from the start of cow’s milk feeds, often with blood or mucus, eczema or vomiting.
Wrong - coeliac disease begins gradually after gluten is introduced, not abruptly straight after an episode of gastroenteritis.
Wrong - Giardia can follow travel or contaminated water but does not typically produce acidic stools with positive reducing substances.
Correct - post-enteritis lactase loss gives acidic, frothy stools with positive reducing substances and perianal excoriation.

mcq.stem:
A 2-year-old girl is seen at the Klinik Kesihatan because her weight has crossed two major centile lines downwards over 6 months. She drinks about 6 bottles of sweetened juice a day and refuses most meals. She is active, examination is normal, and her full blood count is normal. Her length is tracking along the 25th centile.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Start oral iron syrup and recheck her haemoglobin and ferritin after four weeks
Cut down juice and sweet drinks, structure meals and refer her to a dietitian
Refer her to the paediatric endocrine clinic for growth hormone stimulation tests
Prescribe cyproheptadine syrup as an appetite stimulant and review in one month
Admit her to the paediatric ward for nasogastric feeding and supervised meals
mcq.e: Large volumes of juice and sweetened drinks fill a toddler’s stomach and push out calorie-dense food, a common non-organic cause of growth faltering. Management is to optimise nutrition and refer to a dietitian, then monitor for catch-up growth. Medication, specialist tests and admission are not first-line in a well child with an obvious dietary cause.
w: Wrong - her full blood count is normal, so iron treatment has no indication.
Correct - removing the drinks that displace food and getting individual dietitian advice addresses the cause.
Wrong - her length is tracking normally; growth hormone testing is for poor linear growth.
Wrong - appetite stimulants are not recommended and do nothing about the dietary cause.
Wrong - admission is for severe malnutrition, dehydration or failure of outpatient management.

mcq.stem:
A 2-year-old boy is brought to the Klinik Kesihatan because a relative called him ‘too small’. His weight and length are both on the 3rd centile and his head circumference is on the 25th centile. His Child Health Record Book shows that weight and length have tracked steadily along the 3rd centile since birth. His mother is 148 cm and his father 158 cm tall. He eats well, has normal development and a normal examination.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Order thyroid function tests and a bone age X-ray
Refer him to a dietitian for a high-calorie diet
Request a full blood count and serum ferritin
Reassure and continue routine growth monitoring
Refer him to a paediatrician for growth faltering
mcq.e: Growth faltering is judged on the growth trend, not on one measurement. A child who grows steadily along a low centile, with short parents, normal development and a normal examination, is most likely constitutionally or familially small and is not faltering. Reassurance with continued plotting at routine visits avoids needless tests.
w: Wrong - thyroid tests are for poor linear growth with a falling centile or hypothyroid features, neither of which is present.
Wrong - he is not undernourished; extra calories would only raise his weight-for-length.
Wrong - blood tests are not needed for a well child tracking a centile with no clinical concern.
Correct - steady growth along a low centile in keeping with short parents is normal, so plotting should simply continue.
Wrong - a stable centile without crossing lines does not meet the definition of growth faltering.

mcq.stem:
A 7-month-old girl is seen at the Klinik Kesihatan because her weight has fallen from the 50th to the 9th centile. Her mother says she takes 20-30 minutes to finish a small feed and sweats during feeds. Her respiratory rate is 62/min and heart rate 168/min. There is a grade 3/6 pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge and the liver is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Increase the formula’s caloric density and review her weight in four weeks
Refer her to a dietitian for an individualised infant feeding plan
Send urinalysis and urine culture to exclude an occult urinary tract infection
Refer her urgently to the paediatric team for cardiac assessment and echocardiography
Send stool for reducing substances and start a lactose-free formula
mcq.e: Sweating and tiring with feeds, tachypnoea, tachycardia, a pansystolic murmur and hepatomegaly indicate heart failure, probably from a large ventricular septal defect. This is an organic cause that needs urgent paediatric assessment and echocardiography, not nutritional adjustment alone. Systemic examination is what separates organic from non-organic growth faltering.
w: Wrong - extra calories help but do not treat heart failure, and a 4-week delay is unsafe.
Wrong - dietitian input is supportive; the underlying cardiac cause must be dealt with first.
Wrong - UTI is a cause of growth faltering, but these signs clearly point to the heart.
Correct - signs of heart failure with a murmur need urgent cardiac assessment and echo.
Wrong - she has no diarrhoea, so lactose intolerance does not fit.

mcq.stem:
A 2-year-old boy is brought to the Klinik Kesihatan by his mother, who appears flat and tearful. His weight has fallen from the 25th to below the 3rd centile over 8 months. He is unkempt, has severe nappy rash and has missed two vaccination visits. He is watchful and withdrawn, but eats a packet of biscuits ravenously while waiting. There is no diarrhoea, vomiting or recurrent infection, and systemic examination is normal.
Which cause of his growth faltering is most likely?
o: Neglect with inadequate food provision at home
Coeliac disease with hidden malabsorption
Acquired hypothyroidism with poor appetite
Chronic kidney disease with renal tubular acidosis
Genetic syndrome with global developmental delay
mcq.e: Neglect is a non-organic cause of growth faltering. Poor hygiene, missed immunisations, a watchful withdrawn child who eats ravenously when food is offered, and a carer who may be depressed all point to inadequate care and food provision. Organic causes are unlikely with no gastrointestinal or systemic features, and the case needs safeguarding action as well as nutritional support.
w: Correct - poor hygiene, missed visits, ravenous eating and a struggling carer point to neglect.
Wrong - coeliac disease causes poor appetite, abdominal distension and loose stools, not ravenous eating.
Wrong - hypothyroidism slows linear growth with preserved weight and does not explain poor hygiene or missed care.
Wrong - renal disease would give polyuria, vomiting or abnormal urine and is not suggested here.
Wrong - he has no dysmorphic features or delay to suggest a genetic syndrome.

mcq.stem:
A 5-day-old boy is seen at a Klinik Kesihatan postnatal home visit. He has upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, a flat nasal bridge, a single palmar crease and marked hypotonia. Karyotyping was sent before discharge. He is pink, feeding adequately, his oxygen saturation is 98% and no murmur is heard.
What is the most appropriate plan for cardiac assessment?
o: Arrange echocardiography only if a murmur is heard at the 6-week review
Do an ECG and chest X-ray at 6 months and arrange echo only if abnormal
Rely on pulse oximetry and skip echo while saturations stay above 95%
Defer cardiac imaging until school entry, before he joins sports at school
Arrange echocardiography by 6 weeks of age even though no murmur is heard
mcq.e: About half of babies with Down syndrome have congenital heart disease, most typically an atrioventricular septal defect, which may cause no murmur in the first weeks while pulmonary pressure is still high. The Malaysian protocol is echocardiography for every baby with Down syndrome by 6 weeks of age, or earlier if there are abnormal findings. A normal examination and normal saturations do not exclude a defect.
w: Wrong - an AVSD may be silent early, so waiting for a murmur risks missing it.
Wrong - 6 months is too late; pulmonary vascular disease may already be developing.
Wrong - normal saturations do not exclude a left-to-right shunt.
Wrong - this delay could allow irreversible pulmonary hypertension.
Correct - all babies with Down syndrome need an echo by 6 weeks, whatever the examination shows.

mcq.stem:
A 1-week-old girl with clinical features of Down syndrome is reviewed at the Klinik Kesihatan. Postnatal karyotyping has been sent and an echocardiogram is booked for week 5. Her newborn hearing screen was a pass. The medical officer reviews which baseline blood tests are still outstanding.
Which baseline blood tests should be done now?
o: Lateral flexion-extension cervical spine X-rays
Full blood count and thyroid function (T4/TSH)
Coeliac serology with tTG-IgA and total serum IgA
Fasting lipid profile and glycated haemoglobin
Serum ferritin and haemoglobin electrophoresis
