mcq.e: The Malaysian protocol lists FBC and T4/TSH at birth or at 1-2 weeks as the baseline tests. FBC looks for polycythaemia and transient abnormal myelopoiesis, and thyroid function detects congenital hypothyroidism, both more common in Down syndrome. Neck imaging and coeliac screening are not routine newborn baseline tests.
w: Wrong - routine neck X-rays are not recommended; atlantoaxial instability is watched for clinically.
Correct - FBC and T4/TSH at birth or 1-2 weeks are the baseline tests in the protocol.
Wrong - coeliac screening is only considered later in childhood, when symptoms suggest it.
Wrong - metabolic screening has no role in a newborn.
Wrong - these tests are for iron deficiency and haemoglobinopathy, not Down syndrome surveillance.

mcq.stem:
An 8-year-old boy with Down syndrome is brought to the Klinik Kesihatan with 2 weeks of neck pain and a head tilt. His mother says he now walks clumsily and has started wetting himself during the day. On examination he has brisk lower-limb reflexes, ankle clonus and upgoing plantar responses.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Refer him to physiotherapy for torticollis stretching
Give a 1-week course of NSAIDs and review the neck pain
Immobilise the neck and refer urgently for MRI of the spine
Book a routine orthopaedic clinic appointment in 3 months
Start oral baclofen for lower-limb spasticity and review in 2 weeks
mcq.e: Neck pain, head tilt, new gait disturbance, loss of bladder control and upper motor neurone signs in Down syndrome suggest atlantoaxial instability with spinal cord compression. This is an emergency: protect the neck and refer urgently for MRI and specialist spinal care. Neck manipulation or a delayed review risks permanent cord injury.
w: Wrong - stretching the neck could worsen cord compression.
Wrong - pain relief alone ignores the upper motor neurone signs of cord compression.
Correct - cord compression signs need neck immobilisation and urgent MRI with spinal referral.
Wrong - a 3-month wait is unsafe when neurology is progressing.
Wrong - this treats the symptom and misses a compressive cause that needs surgery.

mcq.stem:
A 4-year-old girl with Down syndrome is brought to the Klinik Kesihatan with 3 weeks of tiredness, pallor and leg pains that wake her at night. She has bruises on her shins and back and petechiae on her chest. Her liver is palpable 4 cm and her spleen 3 cm below the costal margins, and there are small cervical lymph nodes. She is afebrile.
Which diagnosis is most likely?
o: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura after a viral infection
Iron deficiency anaemia from poor intake
Physical abuse with multiple bruises of different ages
Acute leukaemia causing bone marrow failure
Acquired hypothyroidism with anaemia of chronic disease
mcq.e: Children with Down syndrome have a markedly increased risk of leukaemia. Pallor, bruising and petechiae (marrow failure), bone pain and hepatosplenomegaly with lymphadenopathy together point to acute leukaemia and need same-day referral for FBC and blood film. ITP causes isolated bleeding in an otherwise well child without organomegaly.
w: Wrong - ITP gives bruising and petechiae in a well child, without pallor, bone pain or organomegaly.
Wrong - iron deficiency explains pallor but not bruising, bone pain or hepatosplenomegaly.
Wrong - abuse would not explain petechiae, pallor and organomegaly; always consider a bleeding or marrow cause first.
Correct - marrow failure, bone pain and organomegaly in a child with Down syndrome strongly suggest acute leukaemia.
Wrong - hypothyroidism causes tiredness but not petechiae, bone pain or hepatosplenomegaly.

mcq.stem:
A 10-year-old boy with Down syndrome attends his yearly review at the Klinik Kesihatan. Over 6 months he has become more tired, gained 4 kg, is constipated and his teacher reports slower work. His height has dropped from the 50th to the 25th centile on the Down syndrome-specific chart. He snores mildly but has no witnessed apnoeas.
Which investigation should be done first?
o: Thyroid function test (free T4 and TSH)
Overnight polysomnography (sleep study)
MRI brain to look for early neurodegeneration
Electroencephalogram to exclude absence seizures
Coeliac serology with tTG-IgA and total IgA level
mcq.e: Hypothyroidism is common throughout life in Down syndrome, which is why thyroid function is checked at least yearly. Weight gain, tiredness, constipation, slower school work and a falling height centile are typical. Its onset is easily mistaken for the expected learning difficulty, so it must be tested for rather than assumed.
w: Correct - weight gain, lethargy, constipation and slowing growth in Down syndrome suggest hypothyroidism.
Wrong - mild snoring without apnoeas does not explain weight gain, constipation and slower growth.
Wrong - the Alzheimer-type decline seen in Down syndrome occurs in adults, not in a 10-year-old.
Wrong - absences cause brief staring spells, not weight gain and constipation.
Wrong - coeliac disease usually causes weight loss and diarrhoea, not weight gain and constipation.

mcq.stem:
A 28-year-old mother attends the Klinik Kesihatan with her 2-month-old daughter, who has Down syndrome. The karyotype report reads 46,XX,t(14;21), showing a Robertsonian translocation. The parents plan another pregnancy and ask about the risk of it happening again.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Reassure them that the recurrence risk is about 1%, as for any young mother
Advise that prenatal testing is not needed because recurrence is unlikely
Offer chromosomal analysis to both parents with genetic counselling
Repeat the baby’s karyotype at 1 year to confirm the translocation
Advise that the risk depends only on the mother’s age at conception
mcq.e: About 4% of Down syndrome is caused by a Robertsonian translocation, and in up to a third of these cases a parent is a balanced carrier. The recurrence risk then is much higher than the roughly 1% after free trisomy 21, especially if the mother is the carrier. Both parents should therefore be karyotyped and offered genetic counselling.
w: Wrong - the roughly 1% figure applies to free trisomy 21, not to a translocation that may be inherited.
Wrong - if a parent carries the translocation, the risk is high and prenatal testing should be offered.
Correct - parental karyotyping shows whether a balanced carrier is present, which sets the true recurrence risk.
Wrong - the baby’s karyotype does not change; the uncertainty lies with the parents.
Wrong - maternal age affects free trisomy 21; the translocation risk depends on carrier status.

mcq.stem:
An 8-year-old boy is referred to the Klinik Kesihatan by his teacher, who completed a rating scale showing 7 inattentive and 6 hyperactive-impulsive symptoms for the past year. His parents report that at home and at religious classes he is calm, follows instructions and completes tasks. His grades fell this year after he moved to a new school where he says older boys tease him.
What is the best interpretation?
o: Combined-type ADHD is confirmed because the teacher reports enough symptoms
Hyperactive-impulsive ADHD is confirmed because symptoms began before age 12
A methylphenidate trial should be given to confirm or exclude ADHD
Oppositional defiant disorder is likely because his behaviour is worse at school
ADHD is not supported because symptoms are not present in two or more settings
mcq.e: Diagnosis needs symptoms that are persistent and pervasive (present in two or more settings), cause functional impairment, and are not better explained by another condition. Symptoms confined to one school after a move and possible bullying point to a situational cause. Look for bullying, learning difficulty, hearing or vision problems before labelling ADHD.
w: Wrong - one informant from one setting is not enough; pervasiveness is required.
Wrong - onset before 12 is necessary but not sufficient without symptoms in two or more settings.
Wrong - a response to stimulants neither confirms nor excludes ADHD; diagnosis is clinical.
Wrong - ODD means angry, defiant behaviour towards adults; this boy is calm and compliant at home.
Correct - symptoms in one setting only, with a clear stressor, do not meet the pervasiveness criterion.

mcq.stem:
A 5-year-old boy has been diagnosed with combined-type ADHD by the paediatrician. His kindergarten complains that he runs around the class and cannot wait his turn. His parents ask the Klinik Kesihatan doctor to start medication so that he settles before primary school. He has no tics, no cardiac history and normal growth.
What is the most appropriate first-line management?
o: Start oral methylphenidate in a low dose and increase it slowly over several weeks
Psychoeducation and parent training, with family and school behavioural support
Start oral atomoxetine because non-stimulants are safer in preschool-aged children
Start oral risperidone at night to reduce his hyperactivity and his impulsivity
Start oral melatonin at bedtime to improve his sleep and his daytime concentration
mcq.e: The Malaysian ADHD CPG recommends medication for children aged 6 years and above and adolescents. In a preschool child, the first line is non-pharmacological: psychoeducation, parent training and family- and school-based behavioural strategies. Medication may be considered later if impairment persists after school entry.
w: Wrong - stimulants are offered from 6 years of age; behavioural management comes first in a 5-year-old.
Correct - psychoeducation with parent, family and school behavioural interventions is first-line under 6 years.
Wrong - atomoxetine is also a medication and the same age threshold applies.
Wrong - antipsychotics are not ADHD treatment and carry metabolic risks.
Wrong - melatonin is for proven sleep-onset problems, not for core ADHD symptoms.

mcq.stem:
A 7-year-old girl is seen at the Klinik Kesihatan because her mother and teacher are concerned about poor attention and fidgeting at home and at school. The medical officer wants a standardised ADHD rating scale that can be completed separately by the parent and the teacher before referral.
Which tool is most appropriate?
o: Social Communication Questionnaire
Vanderbilt ADHD Rating Scale
Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers
Childhood Autism Rating Scale
Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale
mcq.e: The Vanderbilt ADHD Rating Scale has parent and teacher versions that map onto DSM-5 symptoms and also screen for comorbid ODD, conduct and anxiety problems. Conners’ scales, CBCL and SDQ are alternatives listed in the CPG. The other tools screen for or rate autism or maternal depression.
w: Wrong - the SCQ is a parent questionnaire for autism in children over 4 years.
Correct - Vanderbilt has parent and teacher versions covering the DSM-5 ADHD symptoms.
Wrong - M-CHAT is an autism screen for toddlers at 18-24 months.
Wrong - CARS is an observation-based autism rating scale.
Wrong - EPDS screens mothers for postnatal depression.

mcq.stem:
A 9-year-old boy with ADHD started methylphenidate 3 months ago and his school behaviour has improved. His mother says he now eats little at lunch. At the Klinik Kesihatan, his weight has fallen from the 50th to the 25th centile. He has no chest pain, palpitations or tics.
Which parameters must be monitored at every review while he takes this drug?
o: Full blood count and liver function every 3 months
12-lead ECG and echocardiogram at every visit
Serum methylphenidate level before each dose change
Thyroid function and fasting glucose every 6 months
Height, weight, blood pressure and heart rate
mcq.e: Stimulants suppress appetite and can slow weight gain and growth, and they raise blood pressure and heart rate. So height and weight are plotted, and blood pressure and pulse are measured, at every review. Routine blood tests, drug levels and repeated ECGs are not required without a specific indication.
w: Wrong - methylphenidate does not need routine haematology or liver monitoring.
Wrong - an ECG is only for those with cardiac history or symptoms, not routinely at every visit.
Wrong - dosing is titrated by clinical response; serum levels are not used.
Wrong - stimulants do not cause thyroid or glucose problems that need routine checks.
Correct - appetite, growth and cardiovascular effects are tracked by height, weight, BP and pulse.

mcq.stem:
A 10-year-old boy with ADHD attends the Klinik Kesihatan. For 8 months he has often lost his temper, argued with his parents and teachers, refused to follow rules, blamed others for his mistakes and deliberately annoyed his sister. He has not been physically aggressive, damaged property, stolen or run away.
Which comorbid condition is most likely?
o: Oppositional defiant disorder
Conduct disorder
Chronic tic disorder
Generalised anxiety disorder
Early-onset paediatric bipolar disorder
mcq.e: Oppositional defiant disorder is a common ADHD comorbidity: a pattern of at least 6 months of angry or irritable mood, argumentative and defiant behaviour, and vindictiveness. Conduct disorder requires more serious violation of others’ rights, such as aggression, property destruction, theft or serious rule breaking. The absence of these features separates ODD from conduct disorder.
w: Correct - persistent anger, arguing and defiance without serious violation of others’ rights fits ODD.
Wrong - conduct disorder needs aggression, property destruction, theft or serious rule breaking.
Wrong - tics are sudden repeated movements or sounds, not defiant behaviour.
Wrong - anxiety gives worry and avoidance rather than deliberate annoyance of others.
Wrong - bipolar disorder needs distinct episodes of elevated mood; his irritability is constant and directed at authority.

mcq.stem:
A 7-year-old girl is brought to the Klinik Kesihatan because her teacher says she is ‘always daydreaming’. Her mother has noticed episodes many times a day in which she stops talking, stares blankly with fluttering eyelids for about 10 seconds, then carries on as if nothing happened. She has no memory of them. One episode is triggered in clinic when she is asked to breathe deeply for 2 minutes.
Which diagnosis is most likely?
o: Inattentive-type ADHD
Hearing impairment
Specific reading disorder
Childhood absence epilepsy
Childhood depression
mcq.e: Brief, frequent staring spells with eyelid flutter, sudden onset and offset, no memory of the event and provocation by hyperventilation are typical of childhood absence epilepsy. This is a key condition that mimics inattentive ADHD, which is why history and examination must exclude physical causes first. Refer for an EEG, which shows 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges.
w: Wrong - inattentive children drift off but can be redirected; they do not have abrupt spells brought on by hyperventilation.
Wrong - hearing loss causes apparent inattention but not eyelid flutter or episodes triggered by hyperventilation.
Wrong - a reading disorder affects decoding of written words, not consciousness.
Correct - frequent brief absences with eyelid flutter, triggered by hyperventilation, are classic absence epilepsy.
Wrong - depression causes low mood and withdrawal, not brief episodic loss of awareness.

mcq.stem:
A 2-year-old boy is brought to the Klinik Kesihatan because he uses no words, rarely makes eye contact, does not respond when his name is called and spends long periods lining up his toy cars. He was born at term with no complications. He is referred for a developmental assessment.
Which investigation is recommended for every child with suspected autism?
o: Electroencephalogram (EEG)
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
Formal audiological assessment
Thyroid function test
Serum blood lead level
mcq.e: The Malaysian ASD CPG recommends an audiological test for every child with suspected ASD, because hearing impairment can mimic poor response to name and delayed speech. Other investigations, such as EEG, imaging or metabolic and genetic tests, are guided by specific clinical features (seizures, dysmorphism, regression), not done routinely.
w: Wrong - EEG is only indicated if seizures or regression suggest epilepsy.
Wrong - brain imaging is not routine without focal signs, abnormal head size or seizures.
Correct - hearing must be tested in every child with suspected ASD to exclude deafness.
Wrong - thyroid tests are not part of routine ASD work-up without clinical features.
Wrong - lead testing is only for those with pica or exposure risk, not routine.

mcq.stem:
A 30-month-old boy is brought to the Klinik Kesihatan because he says only about 5 words. He makes good eye contact, points to show his mother an aeroplane, brings toys to share, waves bye-bye, follows simple commands and plays pretend tea parties with his sister. Gross and fine motor milestones are normal and he passed a formal hearing assessment last month.
Which diagnosis is most likely?
o: Autism spectrum disorder with associated language impairment
Expressive language delay with intact social skills
Global developmental delay affecting all domains
Undetected sensorineural hearing impairment
Selective mutism related to an anxiety disorder
mcq.e: The key difference between autism and an isolated language delay is social communication. This boy shows joint attention (pointing to share, bringing toys), gestures, comprehension and pretend play, which argues strongly against ASD. With normal hearing and other domains, this is an expressive language delay that still needs speech therapy referral.
w: Wrong - ASD involves impaired joint attention, gestures and pretend play, all of which are intact here.
Correct - only expressive speech is delayed; social communication, comprehension and play are normal.
Wrong - his motor, social and comprehension milestones are age-appropriate.
Wrong - a recent formal hearing test was normal and he follows spoken commands.
Wrong - selective mutism is speaking normally in some settings but not others; he has few words anywhere.

mcq.stem:
A 3-year-old girl is being assessed at the Klinik Kesihatan for suspected autism. Her mother is 30 years old and her father 38. She was born at 31 weeks’ gestation and spent 5 weeks in the neonatal unit. She received her MMR vaccine on schedule and was breastfed until 2 years. There is no family history of autism.
Which factor in her history is a recognised risk factor for autism?
o: Receiving the MMR vaccine at 12 months
Being breastfed until the age of 2 years
Her father’s age of 38 years at her birth
Her birth at 31 weeks’ gestation
Her mother’s age of 30 years at her birth
mcq.e: The Malaysian ASD CPG lists prematurity below 33 weeks, neonatal encephalopathy, family history, maternal age over 40 and paternal age over 50 as risk factors. Parental ages here are below those thresholds. Large studies have shown no link between MMR and autism, and breastfeeding is not a risk factor.
w: Wrong - large studies show no link between MMR and autism.
Wrong - breastfeeding is protective for many outcomes and is not a risk factor for ASD.
Wrong - paternal age becomes a risk factor above 50 years.
Correct - prematurity below 33 weeks is a listed ASD risk factor.
Wrong - maternal age becomes a risk factor above 40 years.

mcq.stem:
A 9-year-old boy with autism attends the Klinik Kesihatan with his parents. For 3 months he has had daily explosive tantrums, bites his hand and hits his younger brother when his routine changes. A structured behavioural programme at school and at home has been in place for 6 months without enough benefit. He sleeps well and is not hyperactive.
Which medication is the evidence-based short-term option for this irritability?
o: Risperidone
Melatonin
Methylphenidate
Carbamazepine
Diazepam
mcq.e: Atypical antipsychotics such as risperidone are recommended for short-term treatment of severe irritability, aggression and self-injury in ASD when behavioural measures alone are not enough. Weight, metabolic effects and prolactin need monitoring. Melatonin targets sleep and stimulants target hyperactivity, which are not his problems.
w: Correct - risperidone is the listed short-term treatment for severe irritability and aggression in ASD.
Wrong - melatonin is for sleep difficulty, and he sleeps well.
Wrong - methylphenidate treats comorbid hyperactivity, which he does not have.
Wrong - carbamazepine is an anticonvulsant without a role for ASD irritability unless seizures are present.
Wrong - benzodiazepines sedate, can cause paradoxical agitation and are not ASD treatment.

mcq.stem:
A 6-year-old boy is seen at the Klinik Kesihatan because his Year 1 teacher reports that he plays alone, does not join in conversation and becomes very upset when his routine changes. His speech is fluent but he talks only about trains. The medical officer wants a parent-completed screening questionnaire validated for this age before referral.
Which tool is most appropriate?
o: Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers
Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule
Vanderbilt ADHD Rating Scale for parents
Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire
Social Communication Questionnaire (SCQ)
mcq.e: The SCQ is a parent-rated screening questionnaire for children over 4 years and works better in those over 7. The M-CHAT is designed for toddlers at 18-24 months. ADOS is a specialist diagnostic observation tool, not a parent screen. Vanderbilt and SDQ screen mainly for ADHD and general behavioural problems.
w: Wrong - M-CHAT is validated only for toddlers aged about 18-24 months.
Wrong - ADOS is a diagnostic observation by trained clinicians, not a parent questionnaire.
Wrong - Vanderbilt screens for ADHD and its comorbidities, not autism.
Wrong - SDQ is a broad behavioural screen and is not specific for autism.
Correct - the SCQ is the parent-rated autism screen for children over 4 years.

mcq.stem:
A 3-year-old boy has just been diagnosed with autism at the Child Development Centre. At the Klinik Kesihatan his parents say a friend advised a gluten-free, casein-free diet and vitamin injections. They ask which treatment has the best evidence as the core intervention for his social communication difficulties.
What is the best advice?
o: Start a strict gluten-free and casein-free diet for at least one full year
Begin risperidone to treat the core social communication deficits
Early intensive behavioural therapy, speech therapy and parent training
Give high-dose vitamin B6 and magnesium supplements daily for six months
Arrange chelation therapy to remove heavy metals linked to autism
mcq.e: The core of ASD management is non-pharmacological: early intensive behavioural intervention such as Applied Behaviour Analysis, speech and communication therapy, occupational therapy and parent education. Medication treats associated problems such as irritability, hyperactivity or sleep, not the core features. Exclusion diets, megavitamins and chelation lack evidence, and chelation can be dangerous.
w: Wrong - gluten- and casein-free diets have no proven benefit and can cause nutritional deficiency.
Wrong - risperidone treats irritability and aggression, not the core social communication deficits.
Correct - early intensive behavioural intervention with speech therapy and parent training is the core treatment.
Wrong - megavitamin therapy is unproven and may be toxic.
Wrong - chelation is unproven and has caused deaths.

mcq.stem:
An 8-year-old boy is seen at the Klinik Kesihatan because his Year 2 teacher says he is ‘a year behind’ in reading. He reads slowly, guesses at unfamiliar words, spells poorly and often confuses b and d. He solves mental sums quickly and answers questions well when material is read to him. Hearing and vision tests are normal and his development was otherwise normal.
Which diagnosis is most likely?
o: Dysgraphia
Dyscalculia
Dyslexia
Inattentive-type ADHD
Mild intellectual disability
mcq.e: Dyslexia is a specific difficulty with decoding, spelling and reading fluency in a child of normal intelligence, often with letter reversals. Good oral comprehension and good arithmetic show that general ability is intact, which argues against intellectual disability. Dysgraphia affects handwriting and written expression rather than reading itself.
w: Wrong - dysgraphia affects handwriting and written work, not reading of text.
Wrong - his arithmetic is a strength, so dyscalculia does not fit.
Correct - poor decoding, spelling and reading fluency with letter reversals but good oral comprehension is dyslexia.
Wrong - ADHD would affect attention across all subjects, not reading alone.
Wrong - intellectual disability affects all areas of learning, but his maths and comprehension are good.

mcq.stem:
A 9-year-old girl attends the Klinik Kesihatan with her mother because of failing mathematics. She reads fluently and enjoys stories, but cannot recall simple addition facts, counts on her fingers, struggles to tell the time and cannot work out change at the shop. Her vision, hearing and general development are normal.
Which intervention is most appropriate?
o: Intensive teaching with concrete materials and counting drills
Phonological awareness training and early decoding practice
Occupational therapy for fine motor and pencil-grip skills
Methylphenidate trial to improve her attention during mathematics
Repeated oral reading programme in a small teaching group
mcq.e: Difficulties with number sense, arithmetic facts, calculation, time and money in a child who reads well indicate dyscalculia. Management is intensive teaching using varied techniques and concrete materials, with practice in counting and number skills. Phonological and reading programmes target dyslexia, and occupational therapy targets dysgraphia.
w: Correct - dyscalculia is managed with intensive multi-technique teaching using concrete materials.
Wrong - phonological training is the intervention for dyslexia.
Wrong - occupational therapy addresses the motor writing problem in dysgraphia.
Wrong - there is no evidence of ADHD; her difficulty is specific to numbers.
Wrong - repeated oral reading builds reading fluency in dyslexia.

mcq.stem:
A 10-year-old boy is referred to the Klinik Kesihatan because his written work is illegible and very slow. He grips his pencil awkwardly, letters vary in size and spacing, and his written stories are disorganised, although he tells the same stories clearly out loud. He reads at his grade level and does well in oral tests. His teacher thinks he is lazy.
Which referral is most appropriate?
o: Speech-language therapy for an articulation disorder
Phonological intervention for a reading disorder
Child psychiatry for a methylphenidate trial
Occupational therapy for handwriting difficulty
Remedial mathematics using concrete materials
mcq.e: Poor handwriting, awkward grip, irregular letter formation and disorganised written work, with good reading and oral expression, suggest dysgraphia. It reflects a problem with the fine motor and organising skills needed to write, not low intelligence or motivation. Management is occupational therapy, with physical therapy where needed.
w: Wrong - his speech is clear; the problem is written output.
Wrong - he reads at grade level, so phonological intervention for dyslexia is not needed.
Wrong - there are no features of ADHD to justify medication.
Correct - dysgraphia is managed with occupational therapy, with physical therapy if needed.
Wrong - concrete-material maths teaching is for dyscalculia.

mcq.stem:
A 6-year-old girl in her first year of school is reviewed at the Klinik Kesihatan. Her mother says she mispronounces long words, cannot learn rhyming nursery songs and shows no interest in letters or their sounds, while her classmates have started to read. Her father had difficulty learning to read. Hearing and vision are normal.
What is the most appropriate intervention?
o: Occupational therapy for handwriting and pencil control
Coloured overlays and tinted lenses for reading tasks
Reassurance and review again when she reaches 9 years
Methylphenidate to improve her attention during lessons
Phonological intervention with alphabet and decoding work
mcq.e: Poor rhyming, mispronunciation and lack of interest in letters and sounds, with a family history, are early signs of dyslexia. The evidence-based approach is early phonological intervention (phonological awareness, alphabet knowledge and early decoding) in individual or small-group teaching. Waiting delays help during the period of greatest benefit.
w: Wrong - occupational therapy is for dysgraphia, not phonological difficulty.
Wrong - coloured overlays have no good evidence in dyslexia.
Wrong - a wait-and-see approach loses the benefit of early intervention.
Wrong - she has no attention problem; her difficulty is with speech sounds.
Correct - phonological awareness, alphabet and decoding work is the first-line dyslexia intervention.

mcq.stem:
A 2-year-old boy with global developmental delay lives in a rural village 3 hours from the nearest hospital. His parents work on a plantation and cannot attend weekly therapy at the Child Development Centre. The Klinik Kesihatan medical officer looks for a government programme near his home that offers early stimulation, motor and self-care training, with home-based support.
Which programme is most suitable?
o: Child Development Centre (CDC) at a tertiary hospital
Program Pemulihan Dalam Komuniti (PDK) run under JKM
Genius Kurnia early intervention programme for autism
Special Education Integration Programme (PPKI) at school
Hospital paediatric rehabilitation outpatient clinic
mcq.e: PDK (community-based rehabilitation) is run under the Department of Social Welfare (JKM) and provides local early stimulation, motor coordination, cognitive readiness and self-care training for young children with disabilities, with home-based support. It suits families who cannot travel to hospital-based services. Genius Kurnia is specific to autism, and PPKI is a school-age education programme.
w: Wrong - CDCs are tertiary hospital units, which the family cannot reach regularly.
Correct - PDK offers community-based and home-based early intervention close to where the family lives.
Wrong - Genius Kurnia is for children with ASD aged 2-6, and this child has global delay.
Wrong - PPKI is a Ministry of Education programme for school-aged children.
Wrong - hospital rehabilitation clinics need the regular hospital attendance this family cannot manage.

mcq.stem:
A 3-year-old boy was diagnosed with autism at the Child Development Centre last month. At the Klinik Kesihatan his mother asks whether there is a government-funded preschool early intervention programme designed for children with his diagnosis, using applied behavioural intervention and involving parent training.
Which programme best fits her request?
o: Genius Kurnia (formerly PERMATA Kurnia)
Program Pemulihan Dalam Komuniti (PDK)
Special Education Integration Programme (PPKI)
Special Education Service Centre (3PK)
Klinik Kesihatan Ibu dan Anak (KKIA) screening
mcq.e: Genius Kurnia, formerly PERMATA Kurnia, is a government-funded early intervention and preschool programme for children with ASD aged 2 to 6, emphasising applied behavioural intervention and parent training. PDK serves children with any disability through community-based rehabilitation. PPKI and 3PK are Ministry of Education services for school-aged pupils.
w: Correct - Genius Kurnia provides ASD-specific early intervention and preschool for ages 2 to 6.
Wrong - PDK is general community-based rehabilitation for any disability, not ASD-specific.
Wrong - PPKI provides special classes in mainstream schools for school-aged pupils.
Wrong - 3PK is a Ministry of Education service centre supporting pupils with special needs.
Wrong - the KKIA is the screening gateway that identifies and refers children; it does not run the programme.

mcq.stem:
A 22-month-old boy is seen at the Klinik Kesihatan for a routine visit. He says only 2 words, although he follows simple commands, points to show interest and plays with other children. A recent hearing test was normal. His grandmother says his father did not talk until 3 years and suggests waiting.
What is the most appropriate action?
o: Reassure and review at 3 years, as late talking runs in the family
Review at the 4-year visit and refer if he is not using sentences
Advise daily educational videos to help build his vocabulary
Refer once he starts kindergarten so that teachers can assess him
Refer now for speech-language assessment and early intervention
mcq.e: Early intervention programmes stress that a child who is not meeting milestones should not be managed by ‘wait and see’. Early identification leads to early support and better developmental outcomes, because the first years are a period of rapid brain development. A family history of late talking does not justify delaying referral.
w: Wrong - waiting loses the period when intervention gives the most benefit.
Wrong - this delays help by more than 2 years.
Wrong - screen time does not build language and is linked with poorer outcomes.
Wrong - kindergarten entry is too late and teachers cannot provide therapy.
Correct - delayed speech warrants prompt referral for speech therapy and early intervention.

mcq.stem:
A 6-month-old boy is brought to the Klinik Kesihatan by his father with bleeding from the mouth. The upper labial frenulum is torn and there is a bruise on the left ear. The father says the baby fell forward while sitting on the floor this morning. The baby cannot yet crawl. He is alert and feeding.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Apply pressure, give paracetamol and review him at the clinic in 3 days
Ask both parents to return together tomorrow for a joint interview
Refer the same day to the hospital paediatric team for SCAN assessment
Lodge a police report and allow the infant to go home with his father
Arrange an outpatient skeletal survey and review the films in 2 weeks
mcq.e: A torn frenulum and ear bruising in a baby who is not yet mobile are red flags for physical abuse, especially with a history that does not fit his development. The child needs same-day referral to the hospital paediatric team and SCAN team for full assessment and protection. Sending the child home or delaying investigations can expose him to further harm.
w: Wrong - treating the wound alone misses possible abuse and leaves the child at risk.
Wrong - delaying assessment risks further injury; carers are interviewed as part of the SCAN process.
Correct - a torn frenulum and ear bruising in a non-mobile infant require same-day SCAN referral.
Wrong - the child’s safety and medical assessment come first; sending him home is unsafe.
Wrong - investigations should be done urgently through the paediatric team, not after a 2-week delay.

mcq.stem:
A 10-month-old girl is referred from the Klinik Kesihatan to the paediatric ward with bruises of different colours on her back, buttocks and thighs. Her mother says she bruises easily, but the explanation changes between carers. There is no family history of bleeding disorder. She is developmentally normal and otherwise well.
Which set of investigations is most appropriate?
o: Skull and cervical spine X-rays, without a full survey
Skeletal survey, platelet count and clotting screen
Isotope bone scan alone, repeated after two weeks
Serum calcium, phosphate and vitamin D levels alone
Abdominal ultrasound and urine toxicology alone
mcq.e: In suspected physical abuse with bruising, the MOH guideline advises a platelet count and coagulation screen to exclude a bleeding disorder, and a skeletal survey in all children under 2 years to find occult fractures. Photographs document the injuries. CT head, abdominal ultrasound and targeted X-rays are added depending on the clinical findings.
w: Wrong - limited films miss occult rib and metaphyseal fractures; a full skeletal survey is needed.
Correct - bruising needs platelets and coagulation, and any child under 2 needs a skeletal survey.
Wrong - a bone scan may complement but does not replace a skeletal survey and bleeding tests.
Wrong - bone chemistry is a second-line test if fractures are found, not the first step.
Wrong - these are only added when there are features of abdominal injury or poisoning.

mcq.stem:
A 3-month-old boy is brought to the Klinik Kesihatan because he has been irritable for 4 days and cries whenever he is lifted under the arms. His mother says there has been no fall or injury. He is referred to hospital, where a skeletal survey is performed.
Which radiological finding would be most specific for non-accidental injury?
o: Healed midshaft clavicle fracture with callus
Spiral fracture of the distal tibial shaft
Buckle fracture of the distal radius
Posterior rib fractures at several levels
Single linear parietal skull fracture
mcq.e: Posterior rib fractures come from forceful squeezing of the chest and are highly specific for abuse in infants, as are metaphyseal corner fractures and multiple fractures of different ages. A clavicle fracture can occur at birth, toddler’s and buckle fractures are typical accidental injuries in walking children, and a single linear skull fracture can follow a short fall.
w: Wrong - a clavicle fracture is a common birth injury and is not specific for abuse.
Wrong - a spiral tibial fracture is a typical accidental injury in a child who is walking.
Wrong - buckle fractures follow falls on an outstretched hand in older children.
Correct - posterior rib fractures from chest squeezing are highly specific for abuse.
Wrong - a single linear skull fracture can follow a minor accidental fall; complex fractures are more suspicious.

mcq.stem:
A 5-month-old girl is transferred from the Klinik Kesihatan to the hospital emergency department after a seizure. She is lethargic, has vomited three times and her anterior fontanelle is bulging. There are no external injuries. Her father says she ‘choked during a feed and went floppy’. She received intramuscular vitamin K at birth and is afebrile. Fundoscopy shows bilateral retinal haemorrhages.
Which investigation should be requested first?
o: Lumbar puncture for CSF microscopy and culture
Electroencephalogram to classify the seizure
Skull X-ray in anteroposterior and lateral views
Abdominal ultrasound to look for free fluid
Non-contrast CT scan of the brain
mcq.e: Seizure, vomiting, lethargy, a bulging fontanelle and retinal haemorrhages without external injury suggest abusive head trauma (shaken baby syndrome) with intracranial bleeding. The MOH guideline lists CT scanning for suspected shaken baby syndrome. Lumbar puncture is dangerous when intracranial pressure may be raised.
w: Wrong - lumbar puncture risks herniation when there are signs of raised intracranial pressure.
Wrong - EEG does not identify the intracranial bleeding that must be found and treated.
Wrong - skull X-rays may show a fracture but miss subdural haemorrhage and brain injury.
Wrong - abdominal ultrasound is for suspected abdominal injury, which is not the main concern here.
Correct - CT brain is the first investigation for suspected abusive head trauma.

mcq.stem:
A 9-year-old boy attends the Klinik Kesihatan with a sore arm. He has several parallel linear bruises in loop shapes on his back and thighs, and admits his stepfather hits him with a belt. His mother begs the doctor not to report it, saying it will break up the family and that it will not happen again.
What is the doctor’s legal obligation?
o: Notify a Protector at JKM at once; reasonable suspicion is enough
Report only if the mother gives written consent to the disclosure
Report only after a forensic examination has proven that abuse occurred
Inform the police within 7 days; there is no need to inform JKM
Keep the matter confidential and review the child again in two weeks
mcq.e: Under Section 27 of the Child Act 2001, a medical officer or registered medical practitioner who believes on reasonable grounds that a child has been abused must immediately inform a Protector (a JKM social welfare officer). Failure to notify is an offence. Parental consent and proof of abuse are not required, and the child’s safety overrides confidentiality.
w: Correct - the Child Act requires immediate notification of a Protector on reasonable grounds.
Wrong - the duty to notify does not depend on parental consent.
Wrong - reasonable suspicion is enough; the doctor does not need to prove abuse.
Wrong - the legal duty is to inform a Protector at JKM, and it must be done immediately.
Wrong - confidentiality does not override child protection, and waiting leaves the child at risk.

mcq.stem:
A 6-year-old girl is brought to the Klinik Kesihatan by her mother 30 hours after she told her mother that an uncle had touched her genitals and ‘hurt her’ while babysitting. She has no bleeding, no discharge and no pain on passing urine, and she is calm.
What is the most appropriate plan for examination?
o: Non-urgent: plan examination after a disclosure interview within the SCAN team
Under anaesthesia: examine in theatre to avoid causing distress to the child
Urgent: refer the same day, as forensic evidence may be lost after 72 hours
Full genital examination at the Klinik Kesihatan by the medical officer first
No examination needed, as physical findings will be absent without symptoms
mcq.e: The MOH guideline treats an acute assault with the last incident within 72 hours as urgent, because forensic evidence may last only hours. The child should be referred the same day to the hospital SCAN team or OSCC. Non-urgent planning applies when the last incident was over 72 hours before, and examination under anaesthesia is reserved for specific indications.
w: Wrong - non-urgent planning is for incidents more than 72 hours before presentation.
Wrong - examination under anaesthesia is for painful injuries, suspected foreign body or a distraught child when examination is essential.
Correct - an incident within 72 hours is urgent because forensic evidence is time-limited.
Wrong - examination should be by a specialist; repeated examinations must be avoided.
Wrong - absence of symptoms never excludes abuse, and evidence collection is time-critical.

mcq.stem:
A 7-year-old girl told her teacher that a neighbour had touched her genitals several times; the last occasion was 3 weeks ago. After a disclosure interview, a specialist examination as part of the SCAN team evaluation finds a normal anogenital examination. At a Klinik Kesihatan follow-up, her mother says, ‘So nothing really happened.’
Which response is most appropriate?
o: Agree, since a normal examination excludes significant sexual abuse
Repeat the genital examination weekly until clear findings appear
Arrange an examination under anaesthesia to look for subtle injury
Explain a normal examination does not exclude abuse; continue protection
Discharge her and advise the mother to watch for any new behaviour changes
mcq.e: The MOH guideline states that absence of physical findings never excludes the possibility of sexual abuse; most abuse leaves no lasting signs, and genital tissues heal quickly. The child’s disclosure remains central, and SCAN evaluation, JKM notification, psychological support and safety planning should continue. Repeated genital examinations must be avoided.
w: Wrong - most sexually abused children have normal examinations, so this cannot exclude abuse.
Wrong - repeated examinations traumatise the child and are specifically to be avoided.
Wrong - anaesthesia is reserved for specific indications such as painful injuries or a suspected foreign body.
Correct - a normal examination never excludes abuse, so protection and support must continue.
Wrong - this leaves the child unprotected despite a credible disclosure.

mcq.stem:
A 15-year-old girl comes to the Klinik Kesihatan with her aunt 20 hours after being raped by an acquaintance. She is tearful but medically stable, with minor bruises on her wrists. She has not bathed or changed clothes. Her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Give emergency contraception at the clinic and review her again after one week
Refer urgently to the hospital OSCC for examination, evidence and prophylaxis
Perform a speculum examination and take high vaginal swabs at the clinic
Tell her a police report must be lodged before she can receive medical care
Refer her first to the psychiatry clinic because of her risk of depression
mcq.e: An adolescent seen within 72 hours of sexual assault should be referred urgently to the hospital One Stop Crisis Centre, where the O&G team examines her, collects forensic evidence and starts emergency contraception, STI antibiotics and HIV post-exposure prophylaxis after counselling. Examination by the specialist avoids repeated examination and preserves evidence. Medical care is never conditional on a police report.
w: Wrong - emergency contraception alone misses forensic evidence, STI and HIV prophylaxis, and crisis support.
Correct - within 72 hours she needs urgent OSCC care with O&G examination, evidence and prophylaxis.
Wrong - examination should be done once by the specialist, so that evidence is preserved and repeat examination avoided.
Wrong - medical care must not be delayed or made conditional on a police report.
Wrong - psychiatric referral is for suicidal risk or depression and follows the acute medical care.
